sections.text:
World Action Models (WAMs) have shown strong potential for robot manipulation by jointly learning visual dynamics and executable actions. However, their video and action objectives do not explicitly constrain the 3D geometry that is crucial for precise manipulation.

Recently, geometry-aware WAMs introduce depth or 4D prediction branches, whereas representation alignment methods supervise intermediate WAM features with pretrained 3D foundation models.

Yet we find that such pointwise alignment benefits the video features but degrades action learning, since dense geometric feature targets overly restrict compact action features.

To address this limitation, we propose Relational Geometry Forcing (RGF), which transfers geometric priors from a frozen 3D foundation model by aligning pairwise feature relations instead of pointwise features.

Specifically, RGF applies three complementary relational objectives, where intra-frame and cross-view relations transfer scene geometry and multi-view correspondence to the video features, while action-temporal relations couple action dynamics to geometric scene evolution.

Applied only during training, RGF requires no explicit geometry branch or extra inference module. Extensive experiments in simulation and the real world demonstrate the effectiveness of Relational Geometry Forcing, showing consistent gains across diverse manipulation scenarios and WAM paradigms.

summary.en: The paper proposes Relational Geometry Forcing (RGF) to transfer geometric priors from a frozen 3D foundation model to World Action Models. Instead of pointwise feature alignment, which the authors say can harm action learning, RGF aligns feature relations through intra-frame, cross-view, and action-temporal objectives. These objectives connect video features to scene geometry and multi-view correspondences, and link action dynamics to geometric scene evolution. RGF is used only in training and adds no explicit geometry branch or inference module. The authors report gains in simulation and real-world manipulation experiments.
summary.zh: 论文提出关系几何约束（RGF），针对点对点几何特征对齐可能损害动作学习的问题，通过对齐特征间关系，将冻结的三维基础模型中的几何先验迁移到世界动作模型。方法以帧内、跨视角及动作时间关系三个目标，分别关联视频特征中的场景几何、多视角对应和动作动态与几何演变。RGF仅用于训练，无需显式几何分支或额外推理模块。作者称，仿真及真实世界实验显示，该方法在多种操作场景和模型范式中均有提升。

sections.text:
Large pretrained robot foundation models provide strong priors for manipulation, yet adapting them to target tasks with offline teleoperated demonstrations often fails to cover the contact-rich, recovery, and precision-critical states encountered during deployment.

Existing methods mitigate this issue by augmenting offline demonstrations with human-in-the-loop data or online reinforcement learning.

Despite this, offline post-training adapts slowly because it cannot immediately absorb deployment experience, while online RL typically relies on value functions or auxiliary actor-critic models, increasing both training complexity and instability. We present TIDE (Training In DEployment), a human-in-the-loop online post-training system.

TIDE introduces a provenance-conditioned supervised learning framework that updates the policy online from human interventions and policy-generated rollouts collected during deployment, without a learned critic, reward model, or action scorer.

Across four real-world bimanual manipulation tasks, TIDE improves milestone-normalized task progress and binary full-task completion over the warm-start policy and matched additional offline demonstrations, and performs comparably to the fixed-policy collection baseline while making updated checkpoints available during deployment.

Each task-specific online post-training session, from the start of deployment rollouts until the final checkpoint is available, completes in less than one hour while learning and checkpoint handling run asynchronously.

summary.en: The paper presents TIDE, a human-in-the-loop system for online robot post-training during deployment. It updates a policy through provenance-conditioned supervised learning from human interventions and policy-generated rollouts, without a learned critic, reward model, or action scorer. In four real-world bimanual manipulation tasks, the authors report improved milestone-normalized progress and full-task completion compared with the warm-start policy and matched additional offline demonstrations. TIDE performs comparably to a fixed-policy collection baseline and provides updated checkpoints during deployment. Each task-specific session takes less than an hour, with learning and checkpoint handling asynchronous.
summary.zh: 论文提出TIDE，一种面向机器人部署过程的人类参与在线后训练系统。它通过带来源信息的监督学习，利用部署期间收集的人类干预和策略生成轨迹在线更新策略，无需学习价值评论器、奖励模型或动作评分器。作者报告，在四项真实世界双臂操作任务中，TIDE相较热启动策略及匹配的额外离线示范，提高了里程碑归一化任务进度和完整任务完成率；其表现与固定策略数据收集基线相当，并能在部署期间提供更新检查点。每项任务的后训练会话不到一小时，学习和检查点处理异步进行。

sections.text:
Long-horizon robot manipulation requires a robot to remember task-relevant information beyond its short observation window. Existing memory-augmented policies typically retrieve relevant information from history and reason over it at execution time, placing a heavy reasoning burden on the high-level model.

To address this challenge, we propose PAL (\textbf{P}lan first, \textbf{A}ct \textbf{L}ater), a hierarchical memory framework for vision-language robot manipulation. It maintains a short-term visual buffer, a semantic-event memory, and an executable \texttt{subtask\_list}.

A high-level vision-language model (VLM) converts streaming visual observations into the \texttt{subtask\_list}.At execution time, the VLM selects the currently relevant subtask from the \texttt{subtask\_list} and passes it to a low-level vision-language-action (VLA) policy.

To teach the model what to write to memory and when to update it, we introduce a two-stage data generation procedure that first expands sparse update supervision and then uses self-labeling with task-grounded verification to generate training data that better match the state distribution encountered during execution.

We evaluate our approach on memory-dependent benchmarks and real-world manipulation tasks. On RoboMME, PAL achieves a \textbf{56.05\%} success rate, outperforming the strongest baseline, FrameSamp-Modul, at 44.51\%.

In real-world experiments across four manipulation tasks, \pal{} reaches \textbf{60.83\%} overall success, surpassing MemER (45.00\%) and FrameSamp-Modul (28.33\%).These results show that proactively writing future-relevant subtasks into hierarchical memory improves long-horizon visual reasoning and robot control.

Code and videos can be found on our website: https://qinghangliu.github.io/pal-webpage/

summary.en: The paper introduces PAL, a hierarchical memory framework for vision-language robot manipulation. It maintains a short-term visual buffer, semantic-event memory, and executable subtask list. A high-level vision-language model builds the list from streaming observations and selects a relevant subtask for a low-level vision-language-action policy at execution time. A two-stage data-generation procedure expands sparse update supervision and uses self-labeling with task-grounded verification. PAL achieves a reported 56.05% success rate on RoboMME, versus 44.51% for the strongest baseline, and 60.83% overall success across four real-world tasks, exceeding the two named baselines.

sections.text:
Factory work is a promising early scenario for embodied AI: assigning repetitive manual jobs to robots has clear economic payoff, and a structured station keeps the jobs tractable for current policies. Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models now dominate as the policy paradigm for these robots.

The inference latency of VLA models directly affects robot responsiveness and motion smoothness. However, existing VLA inference frameworks do not fully exploit the characteristics of embodied workloads or account for the distinct bottlenecks across different stages of VLA inference.

In this paper, we first characterize embodied workloads and identify substantial task similarity across repeated robot executions. We further find that such similarity extends beyond observations and action trajectories to internal model states.

Drawing on these observations, we present rMuscle, a real-time VLA inference framework inspired by human muscle memory. It exploits cross-execution similarity through a dual-phase muscle-memory cache. The Context Cache reuses visual-token outputs to reduce computation, while the Action Cache reuses neuron activation patterns to reduce weight accesses.

We keep both the cache memory footprint and access overhead low through online cache recomputation, sliding-window cache retrieval, and mask sharing across consecutive denoising steps. rMuscle achieves 1.29-1.42X speedup on RTX 4090 and Jetson Thor across LIBERO, RoboTwin, and physical manipulation tasks, while maintaining the original success rates on real-world robots.

summary.en: The paper presents rMuscle, a real-time framework intended to reduce inference latency for vision-language-action models. The authors identify similarity across repeated robot executions, including in internal model states, and use a two-phase cache. The Context Cache reuses visual-token outputs to reduce computation, while the Action Cache reuses neuron activation patterns to reduce weight accesses. Online cache recomputation, sliding-window retrieval, and mask sharing across consecutive denoising steps limit memory footprint and access overhead. The authors report 1.29–1.42× speedups across tasks on RTX 4090 and Jetson Thor, while maintaining original success rates on real-world robots.
summary.zh: 论文介绍rMuscle，一种旨在降低视觉语言动作模型推理延迟的实时框架。作者发现重复机器人执行中的相似性也存在于模型内部状态，并设计双阶段肌肉记忆缓存：上下文缓存复用视觉令牌输出以减少计算，动作缓存复用神经元激活模式以减少权重访问。在线缓存重算、滑动窗口检索和连续去噪步骤间的掩码共享用于控制缓存占用和访问开销。作者报告，该框架在RTX 4090和Jetson Thor上的多类任务中实现1.29至1.42倍加速，并在真实机器人上保持原有成功率。

sections.text:
A central challenge in deploying learned robot policies is inference-time behavior steering: redirecting a policy at test time to satisfy user preferences not anticipated during training, without retraining.

Existing methods fail in two modes: end-to-end methods require fine-tuning or expert-level guidance, while neuro-symbolic methods rely on predefined symbols whose edits can result in logically reasonable but physically infeasible plans.

To address this challenge, we propose ReStruct, which builds upon a neural automaton policy that decomposes a visuomotor policy into a high-level state-machine skeleton capturing task structure and a low-level continuous controller represented as a residual policy.

Specifically, ReStruct adopts the automaton to represent the preference and incorporates it into the skeleton through a synchronous product, thereby reconfiguring the task structure. With the controller kept frozen, the action priors provided by the skeleton are updated accordingly to enable physically-aware control under a modified task structure.

Extensive experiments from simulation and real-world show that ReStruct steers a wide range of preferences, from object-centric specifications to temporal-logic constraints, and after steering surpasses existing methods, exceeding VLA models in both task success and preference-following by up to 25%.

summary.en: The paper presents ReStruct for steering learned robot policies at inference time to meet user preferences without retraining. It represents preferences with an automaton and uses a synchronous product to reconfigure a task-structure skeleton, while keeping the low-level continuous controller frozen. The authors report simulation and real-world experiments covering preferences from object-centric specifications to temporal-logic constraints. After steering, ReStruct surpasses existing methods and exceeds VLA models in task success and preference following by up to 25%.
summary.zh: 论文提出 ReStruct，用于在不重新训练的情况下，于推理阶段按用户偏好调整已学习的机器人策略。方法以神经自动机表示偏好，并通过同步积修改任务结构骨架，同时冻结低层连续控制器，使骨架更新动作先验以支持物理可行的控制。作者报告，仿真和真实世界实验涵盖从对象中心规范到时序逻辑约束的多种偏好；调整后，ReStruct 超过现有方法，并在任务成功和偏好遵循方面较 VLA 模型最高提升 25%。

sections.text:
Legged robots can extend planetary exploration to rugged and discontinuous terrain that is inaccessible to conventional rovers. In lunar gravity, jumping further expands this mobility by enabling robots to cross obstacles and gaps that cannot be traversed by walking alone.

We present a multistage reinforcement-learning approach that produces a single end-to-end control policy for commanded point-to-point jumping under lunar gravity. The resulting policy has a simple architecture and relies exclusively on mission-compatible onboard sensing, making its deployment on a real lunar mission plausible.

In simulation, the learned policy performs accurate point-to-point jumps with landing errors smaller than the robot's body size. We analyze the torque and power demands of lunar jumping and characterize performance degradation under extreme outlier events, including control-update freezes of up to \SI{1}{s} during flight.

Hardware transfer demonstrates that the policy can successfully execute a vertical jump under lunar-gravity offloading. Furthermore, the measured torque and power profiles are consistent with the simulation results and remain within the robot's hardware limits.

summary.en: The paper presents a multistage reinforcement-learning method for a single end-to-end policy controlling quadrupedal point-to-point jumps in lunar gravity. The policy has a simple architecture and uses only mission-compatible onboard sensing. In simulation, landing errors are smaller than the robot's body size; the study also analyzes torque and power demands and degradation under extreme events, including flight-time control-update freezes of up to one second. Hardware transfer demonstrates a vertical jump under lunar-gravity offloading, with measured torque and power profiles consistent with simulation and within hardware limits.

sections.text:
Learning-based path planners based on diffusion and flow matching can generate diverse trajectories from demonstrations but typically lack mechanisms for constraint satisfaction and collision avoidance during deployment.

This work proposes a framework that combines flow-matching-based path planning with model predictive path-following control to integrate data-driven path generation with real-time, constraint-aware execution.

The flow-matching model captures multimodal path distributions, while the predictive controller adapts motion online to satisfy state and input constraints and avoid obstacles using updated local sensor information.

An event-triggered re-planning scheme incorporates predictive control solutions into subsequent path generation, promoting collision-free navigation in environments with previously unseen obstacles. Simulation results for mobile robot navigation demonstrate robust performance across cluttered environments.

The framework provides a systematic approach to combining flow matching with predictive control for adaptive, data-driven navigation.

summary.en: The paper proposes a robot navigation framework that combines flow-matching path planning with model-predictive path-following control. The flow-matching model represents multimodal path distributions, while the predictive controller adjusts motion online using updated local sensor information to meet state and input constraints and avoid obstacles. Event-triggered replanning feeds control solutions into subsequent path generation to handle previously unseen obstacles. Mobile-robot simulation results demonstrate robust performance in cluttered environments; the authors describe the framework as a systematic approach to adaptive, data-driven navigation.
summary.zh: 论文提出一种将流匹配路径规划与模型预测路径跟踪控制结合的机器人导航框架。流匹配模型根据示范捕捉多模态路径分布；预测控制器则利用更新的局部传感信息在线调整运动，以满足状态和输入约束并避开障碍。事件触发式重规划把预测控制的解纳入后续路径生成，旨在应对环境中先前未见的障碍。移动机器人仿真结果显示，该方法在拥挤环境中表现稳健；摘要将其描述为结合数据驱动路径生成与自适应控制的系统方法。

sections.text:
World action models (WAMs) are shown to substantially diverge under generalization performance based on their generative backbones. We investigate this gap through the representational geometry that WAMs inherit from their backbones and how policy training reorganizes it.

Our central hypothesis is that a useful representational prior would structure geometry that separates nuisance information from the in-distribution manifold in advance of training as a policy. We quantify this with nuisance orthogonality; orthogonality of the feature under visual variation outside the empirical in-distribution manifold.

Across various image and video backbones, we show that a higher orthogonality from the representational prior is associated with stronger robustness to visual variations after WAM training, enabling policy generalization measurable prospectively for world models.

In addition, analyzing the resulting robust WAMs reveals nuisance suppression; relative suppression of feature displacement caused by such variations and robust action generation of the policy. Together, these findings provide a geometric perspective on how the representational prior of the world model shapes the generalization performance of WAMs.

summary.en: The paper studies how representational geometry inherited from generative backbones, and its reorganization during policy training, relate to generalization in world action models (WAMs). The authors hypothesize that a useful prior separates nuisance information from the in-distribution manifold before policy training, and quantify this using nuisance orthogonality under visual variation outside that manifold. Across image and video backbones, higher prior orthogonality is associated with stronger robustness after WAM training. Analysis of robust models also reveals nuisance suppression and robust action generation, motivating a geometric account of how priors shape generalization.

sections.text:
In this article, we propose ContactFlowFilter, a novel approach for contact estimation that determines the number of active contacts, their locations, and the associated force vectors.

We consider a robot manipulator equipped with joint torque sensors and a base force/torque sensor; such a proprioceptive-only setup presents a challenging inverse problem characterized by (i) multi-modality from non-unique solutions, (ii) temporal dependencies in state evolution, and (iii) discrete contact events involving contact addition/removal.

Existing approaches, such as particle filters (PFs) and learning-based methods, often struggle to address these challenges simultaneously. To overcome this, ContactFlowFilter integrates a generative model into the PF framework.

The recursive structure of the PF captures temporal dependencies, while the flow matching model serves as an auxiliary proposal distribution to track multi-modal beliefs and detect contact events. Extensive validation in both simulation and real-world experiments confirms the effectiveness of the proposed method.

In real-world settings, ContactFlowFilter achieves the lowest dissimilarity from the target distribution, with errors of only 0.36 cm and 0.88 cm for single- and dual-contact scenarios, respectively, while operating at 0.69 ms and 2.69 ms.

summary.en: The paper presents ContactFlowFilter for online estimation of the number, locations, and force vectors of contacts using only joint torque and base force/torque sensors. It integrates a flow-matching generative model as an auxiliary proposal distribution within a particle filter to address multimodal solutions, temporal dependencies, and contact events. The authors report validation in simulation and real-world experiments. In real-world single- and dual-contact scenarios, they report target-distribution dissimilarities of 0.36 cm and 0.88 cm, with runtimes of 0.69 ms and 2.69 ms, respectively.

sections.text:
Humans typically rely on vision, touch, hearing, and proprioception to perceive contact and adapt their actions during manipulation. Providing robots with comparable responsiveness therefore requires hardware that can retain and use these complementary sensory signals.

Most imitation-learning systems, however, observe demonstrations primarily through vision and proprioception, limiting access to contact information that is difficult to infer visually. We present PolyUMI, an open-source platform for scalable visual--tactile--audio demonstration collection and robot deployment.

Its lightweight, wireless handheld gripper records synchronized wrist-camera, optical tactile, contact-audio, and proprioceptive observations without requiring a tethered workstation. The same sensing finger can be transferred to the robot end effector, preserving the sensing geometry between demonstration collection and policy execution.

To effectively use these heterogeneous observations, we further introduce VisTA, a token-level multimodal policy that integrates information across sensors and time to predict contact-aware robot actions.

Experiments spanning object inference, slip control, and contact-rich manipulation show that touch and audio reveal task-relevant information beyond vision and that VisTA is competitive with or outperforms existing multimodal policies.

Together, PolyUMI and VisTA provide an accessible pipeline for collecting multimodal demonstrations and learning policies that perceive physical interaction beyond vision. Project Page: https://polyumi-vista.github.io

summary.en: The paper introduces PolyUMI, an open-source platform for collecting visual, tactile, and audio demonstrations and deploying robots. Its wireless handheld gripper synchronously records wrist-camera, optical tactile, contact-audio, and proprioceptive data; the same sensing finger can be transferred to a robot end effector to preserve sensing geometry. The authors also present VisTA, a multimodal policy that combines sensor and temporal information to predict contact-aware actions. Experiments in object inference, slip control, and contact-rich manipulation show that touch and audio provide task-relevant information beyond vision, and that VisTA is competitive with or outperforms existing multimodal policies.

sections.text:
Autonomous mobile robots operating in dense crowds and cluttered sites require $360^\circ$ perception to react to surrounding hazards.

While panoramic LiDAR offers full-surround coverage, learning representations within reinforcement learning (RL) is sample-inefficient under sparse rewards, and existing 3D pretrained point-cloud encoders are too memory-heavy for massively parallel RL simulation.

We present RangeNav, a compact (183k parameters) LiDAR range-image encoder pretrained entirely on synthetic data. RangeNav uses anisotropic convolutions and circular padding to handle the extreme aspect ratio and azimuthal seam of range images.

We pretrain the network using a navigation-aligned objective combining range reconstruction, semantic segmentation, and bird's-eye-view (BEV) prediction, then freeze it for policy learning.

In simulation, adding semantic and BEV supervision increases success rates over a reconstruction-only baseline by an average of 32.03 and 23.73 percentage points (pp) in procedurally generated training and out-of-distribution realistic test environments, respectively.

Zero-shot real-world deployments on a Unitree B2-W quadruped demonstrate robust navigation through dense crowds, low-light settings, and construction zones where limited-field-of-view depth policies struggle. Code and models will be open-sourced.

summary.en: The paper presents RangeNav, a compact LiDAR range-image encoder pretrained entirely on synthetic data for robot navigation. Anisotropic convolutions and circular padding address range images' aspect ratio and azimuthal seam. Its pretraining objective combines range reconstruction, semantic segmentation, and bird's-eye-view prediction; the encoder is then frozen for policy learning. In simulation, semantic and BEV supervision raise success rates over a reconstruction-only baseline by average margins of 32.03 and 23.73 percentage points in procedural training and out-of-distribution realistic test environments, respectively. The authors also report zero-shot quadruped deployments navigating dense crowds, low-light settings, and construction zones.
summary.zh: 论文提出 RangeNav，一种在合成数据上预训练的紧凑激光雷达距离图编码器，用于机器人导航。其各向异性卷积和循环填充适配距离图的长宽比及方位接缝；预训练目标结合距离重建、语义分割和鸟瞰图预测，随后冻结编码器进行策略学习。仿真中，相较仅重建基线，语义与鸟瞰监督使程序化训练环境和分布外真实感测试环境的成功率分别平均提高32.03和23.73个百分点。作者还报告四足机器人零样本真实部署可在拥挤人群、低光照和施工区域导航。

sections.text:
Recently, multi-node inertial measurement unit (multi-IMU) systems have shown promise for robust odometry in legged robots. Multi-IMU fusion can improve legged robot odometry but requires accurate spatiotemporal calibration among the sensors.

Existing multi-IMU calibration methods, designed for aerial or handheld platforms, face challenges on legged robots because routine locomotion may provide insufficient excitation, while foot slips, impacts, and vibrations introduce measurement disturbances.

To address these challenges, we propose A2I-Calib++, a kinematics-driven anti-noise active calibration framework for body-mounted IMUs covered by the robot kinematic model.

It estimates temporal offsets, extrinsic rotations and translations, and inertial biases through temporal correlation search followed by analytic spatial and bias estimation, without artificial calibration targets or complex parameter tuning for the target IMU.

A2I-Calib++ comprises three core modules: 1) a Noise-Isotropy-Inspired Trajectory supported by a finite-horizon conditioning proposition that generates sufficient excitation to limit noise sensitivity; 2) a constraint-aware Adversarial Motion Priors controller that combines the anti-noise excitation with a rolling-contact reward for contact-aware execution; and 3) a contact-constrained virtual IMU that fuses pre-calibrated calf IMUs and joint kinematics under a rolling-contact model to construct the calibration reference.

Furthermore, evaluations on both simulation and real-world quadruped platforms demonstrate notably reduced noise sensitivity and simulation calibration errors compared to conventional methods, together with repeatable real-world calibration and improved proprioceptive odometry accuracy for legged robots.

summary.en: The paper presents A2I-Calib++, an active calibration framework for whole-body multi-IMU systems on legged robots. It estimates temporal offsets, extrinsic rotations and translations, and inertial biases using kinematic information. Its components generate excitation, control contact-aware motion, and construct a virtual IMU reference. The authors report evaluations in simulation and on real quadruped platforms, showing lower noise sensitivity and simulation calibration errors than conventional methods, repeatable real-world calibration, and improved proprioceptive odometry accuracy.
summary.zh: 论文提出 A2I-Calib++，一种面向腿式机器人的全身多 IMU 主动标定框架。该方法通过运动学信息估计传感器时间偏移、外参旋转和平移及惯性偏置，并以激励轨迹、考虑接触约束的运动控制和虚拟 IMU 构建应对噪声与足端接触影响。作者报告，仿真和真实四足平台评估显示其噪声敏感性和仿真标定误差较传统方法降低，且真实场景标定具有重复性，本体感知里程计精度有所提升。

items.title: A2I-Calib++: A Kinematics-Driven Anti-noise Active Calibration Framework for Whole-Body Multi-IMU Systems on Legged Robots

sections.text:
In contact-rich manipulation, contact conditions can change before a visual policy updates its action plan. Recomputing the plan through the visual policy adds latency, while tactile feedback alone does not specify how the ongoing motion should be revised for the task.

We introduce T-WLA, a world-language-action architecture that uses shared visual memory to guide both action generation and tactile correction. At each visual update, the visual branch integrates the current image, task instruction, and retrieved history into a visual memory that conditions base-action generation.

The same memory is cached for a lightweight tactile editor, which combines it with the active action chunk and incoming touch to predict residual corrections to unexecuted actions without rerunning the visual branch.

Future-image and future-pressure prediction provide training-only supervision, encouraging the visual memory and tactile features to capture interaction dynamics relevant to action generation and correction. We evaluate T-WLA on tactile-conditioned hand-motion prediction using EgoTouch and Tachin, and on four real-world dexterous manipulation tasks.

T-WLA reduces finger-joint MPJPE by 30% relative to the strongest reported baseline and achieves an average success rate of approximately 50.0% across real-robot manipulation tasks. Videos and code are available at https://anonymous-submission-20.github.io/T-WLA.github.io/.

summary.en: The paper introduces T-WLA, which uses shared visual memory to connect visual action planning with tactile correction. A visual branch uses images, task instructions, and retrieved history to generate base actions; a lightweight tactile editor uses cached memory, the active action chunk, and touch input to correct unexecuted actions without rerunning the visual branch. Future-image and pressure prediction serve only as training supervision. Evaluations include tactile-conditioned hand-motion prediction on EgoTouch and Tachin and four real-world tasks. The authors report a 30% reduction in finger-joint MPJPE versus the strongest reported baseline and about 50% average success across robot tasks.
summary.zh: 论文提出 T-WLA，用共享视觉记忆连接视觉规划与触觉修正：视觉分支根据图像、任务指令和历史生成基础动作，轻量触觉编辑器则利用缓存记忆、当前动作片段和触觉输入，修正尚未执行的动作，无需重新运行视觉分支。未来图像和压力预测仅作为训练监督。作者在 EgoTouch、Tachin 的触觉条件手部动作预测及四项真实灵巧操作任务中评估该架构，报告手指关节 MPJPE 相对最强已报告基线降低 30%，真实机器人任务平均成功率约为 50%。

items.title: T-WLA: Bridging Slow Vision and Fast Touch

sections.text:
World models predict how embodied systems evolve under actions, but their accuracy can degrade when physical conditions move outside the training distribution. We study two components of causal modeling: which inputs a predictor may use, and how its mechanism computes their effects.

In a synthetic benchmark with shortcut features, a frozen dependency mask derived from paired interventions reduces mean out-of-distribution (OOD) RMSE from 1.769 for a fully connected predictor to 0.697, close to the generator-oracle mask (0.694).

For robot link-mass extrapolation in CausalWorld, with disjoint training and test mass ranges, we develop finger-local world models in which link masses enter inertia and dynamics-bias terms through explicit affine coefficients, actions act through either a learned torque network or the known PD controller, and learned residuals capture contact-related effects.

Compared with a separately trained control whose mass inputs are fixed at training means, the known-PD model turns out-of-range masses into a consistent predictive gain: median time-averaged joint R2 over 150-step rollouts rises from 0.609 to 0.727, with improvement in all ten task-seed runs (exact two-sided sign test, p = 0.002).

In a shared 100-step forecast, the learned-torque model is competitive with the strongest recurrent robotic world model (RWM) configuration (median joint R2 of 0.755 - 0.768 versus 0.752), whereas supplying out-of-range masses sharply degrades the MLP and recurrent predictors.

These results indicate that how a physical parameter enters the dynamics mechanism determines whether its out-of-range value helps or harms prediction.

summary.en: The paper studies how input dependencies and the mechanism used to model dynamics affect world-model predictions when physical parameters shift beyond the training range. In a synthetic shortcut-feature benchmark, a frozen dependency mask derived from paired interventions lowers OOD RMSE from 1.769 to 0.697, near the generator-oracle mask’s 0.694. In CausalWorld link-mass extrapolation, a model with known PD control and explicit mass terms raises median joint R² over 150-step rollouts from 0.609 to 0.727. The learned-torque model is competitive with a recurrent model in a shared 100-step forecast. These findings are limited to the reported setups.
summary.zh: 论文研究物理参数超出训练范围时，因果世界模型的输入依赖关系与动力学机制如何影响预测。合成基准中，依据配对干预得到并冻结的依赖掩码，使 OOD RMSE 从全连接预测器的 1.769 降至 0.697，接近生成器预言掩码的 0.694。CausalWorld 连杆质量外推实验中，显式将质量纳入惯性和动力学偏置项的已知 PD 模型，在 150 步预测的中位关节 R² 从 0.609 提升至 0.727。作者还报告学习力矩模型在 100 步预测中与较强循环模型相当；结论限于文中基准与实验设置。

items.title: Causal world models under physical parameter shifts

sections.text:
Currently, dexterous humanoid robot hands are widely considered the final hardware bottleneck that hampers generalist robots from physically assisting people at home and work.

As conventional tendon-driven designs suffer from high cost, demanding maintenance, poor reliability, and short durability, alternative linkage-driven designs have increasingly gained attention.

Despite their potential to avoid the weaknesses of tendon-driven hands, integrating multiple degrees of actuation (DOA) in a single digit with linkage drivetrains is a challenge for design and fabrication.

Only a few studies have managed to present functional humanoid hands that are completely linkage-driven and have at least three DOAs per digit without compromising actuator placement and other design preferences. Our work introduces a new linkage-driven hand featuring a unique flexure hinge.

Together with elastic drive rods made of spring steel, the linkage drivetrains are significantly simplified. Unlike other linkage-driven designs of similar dexterity, our design does not require many miniature moving parts. As a result, the hand can be fabricated easily with a budget 3D printer.

This not only significantly lowers the barrier to entry for using and developing dexterous humanoid robot hand functions, but also allows the hands to be sized much closer to regular human hands. The design offers desirable kinematic advantages as well. A prototype is evaluated for grasping and object manipulation.

In addition, this paper presents our latest findings on kinematics and control of the hand.

summary.en: The paper presents PHD-Hand, a linkage-driven humanoid dexterous hand with three degrees of actuation per digit. A flexure hinge and elastic spring-steel drive rods simplify the linkages and reduce the number of miniature moving parts. The authors say the design can be fabricated with a budget 3D printer, lowering the barrier to developing and using dexterous hand functions and allowing sizing closer to a regular human hand. The paper also reports findings on the hand’s kinematics and control. A prototype was evaluated for grasping and object manipulation, but the abstract gives no specific performance results.
summary.zh: 论文介绍 PHD-Hand，一种采用连杆驱动、每指具有三个驱动自由度的人形灵巧手。设计以独特柔性铰链和弹簧钢弹性驱动杆简化传动结构，减少微型活动零件，并可用预算型 3D 打印机制造。作者称，这有助于降低开发和使用灵巧手的门槛，并使手部尺寸更接近普通人手。论文还讨论其运动学与控制的最新发现；原型机进行了抓取和物体操作评估，但摘要未给出具体性能结果。

items.title: PHD-Hand: A Printable Humanoid Dexterous Hand with Linkage-Driven 3-DOA Digits

sections.text:
With the advent of foundation models, robots are increasingly capable of understanding and executing explicitly specified human tasks. Extending these capabilities to open-ended tasks, however, requires robots to infer appropriate actions from the observed scene.

Household organization exemplifies this challenge, as robots must often act without detailed instructions, predefined object vocabularies, or known object-receptacle associations.

While robots may follow instructions or learn organization preferences from demonstrations, inferring the latent organization of an occasionally changing scene and placing a novel object consistently with it remains challenging.

We propose an open-world multi-attribute reasoning pipeline that grounds unknown objects across views and constructs an instance-level 3D scene graph for placement reasoning. First, a vision-language model proposes labels together with attributes such as content and packaging type, which are grounded through segmentation, depth, and multi-view association.

Then, an LLM reasons over this representation to infer the latent shelf organization and rank scene-consistent object placements without explicitly user-provided preferences. The resulting placement rankings guide subsequent geometric and kinematic feasibility checks for execution.

Our experimental evaluation shows that our approach leads to improved instance mapping and placement coherence over single-view language-grounding and geometry-only baselines, enabling autonomous placement of previously unseen objects without predefined object-receptacle mappings or class-specific retraining.

summary.en: The paper proposes an open-world, multi-attribute reasoning pipeline for shelf organization. A vision-language model proposes object labels and attributes, which are grounded across views to build an instance-level 3D scene graph. An LLM infers latent organization patterns and ranks scene-consistent placements, followed by geometric and kinematic feasibility checks. Experimental evaluation reports improved instance mapping and placement coherence over single-view language-grounding and geometry-only baselines, enabling placement of previously unseen objects without predefined mappings or class-specific retraining.
summary.zh: 论文提出用于货架整理的开放世界多属性推理流程：通过视觉语言模型提出物体标签与属性，并结合分割、深度和多视角关联，将未知物体定位到实例级三维场景图；随后由大语言模型推断场景中潜在的整理规律并排序合适摆放位置，再进行几何与运动学可行性检查。实验评估显示，该方法相较单视角语言定位和仅几何基线，在实例映射和摆放连贯性方面有所改善，并支持整理未见物体。

items.title: OMAR: Open-World Multi-Attribute Reasoning for Scene-Conditioned Shelf Organization

sections.text:
Thermal cameras enable robots to perceive human activities in darkness while revealing less personally identifiable appearance information and fewer details of the surrounding environment than RGB cameras.

As vision-language models (VLMs), originally developed for RGB imagery, are increasingly integrated into embodied systems for scene understanding and high-level planning, thermal sensing offers a promising way to extend activity perception to low-light and privacy-sensitive settings.

However, the failure modes of VLMs in thermal human activity understanding for human-robot interaction (HRI) remain underexplored. We fill this gap by evaluating seven locally deployable VLMs, including models developed for physical AI and robotics, on two person-centric thermal datasets.

Our diagnostic tasks examine fine-grained action recognition, activity timeline reconstruction, and the ability to withhold unsupported answers. Paired RGB recordings serve as a performance reference, while controlled variations in frame sampling, thermal input presentation, and reasoning are used to assess whether the observed errors can be mitigated.

Our results show that models can recognize broad activity categories but struggle with fine-grained actions such as coughing, sneezing, and yawning. They also produce inaccurate event timelines and hallucinate actions involving objects. Simple thermal input preprocessing and additional reasoning offer only limited, model-dependent gains.

Abstention behavior also varies across models even under explicit instructions, limiting their reliability for practical robotic use.

summary.en: The paper evaluates seven locally deployable vision-language models on two person-centric thermal datasets, testing fine-grained action recognition, activity timeline reconstruction, and abstention from unsupported answers, with paired RGB recordings as a reference. Models recognize broad activity categories but struggle with actions such as coughing, sneezing, and yawning, produce inaccurate timelines, and hallucinate object-related actions. Thermal preprocessing and additional reasoning yield only limited, model-dependent gains. Abstention behavior varies across models, which the authors say limits reliability for practical robotic use.
summary.zh: 论文评估了七种可本地部署的视觉语言模型在两组以人为中心的热成像数据集上的活动理解表现，任务包括细粒度动作识别、活动时间线重建和拒绝无依据回答，并以配对 RGB 录像作参考。结果显示，模型能识别宽泛活动类别，但难以区分咳嗽、打喷嚏和打哈欠等细动作，也会生成不准确的事件时间线及涉及物体的虚构动作。热成像输入预处理和额外推理仅带来有限且因模型而异的改善；各模型的弃答表现也不一致。

items.title: Failure Modes of Vision-Language Models for Human Activity Understanding in Thermal HRI

sections.text:
One-step generation from standard diffusion or Flow-Matching training is rarely effective for text-to-image or video generation without distillation or specialized one-step objectives. We find that VLA action generation behaves strikingly differently.

Biasing only the training timestep distribution toward the noise endpoint yields strong one-step policies across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, LIBERO-Pro, and real-world robot tasks.

Moreover, for open-source VLA models with different architectures, simply replacing iterative decoding with a single forward pass often performs comparably to the original multi-step decoding on benchmarks such as LIBERO, CALVIN, and SimplerEnv.

We attribute this difference to the condition-target structure of VLA generation, which is closer to image-to-text than text-to-image: rich observations strongly constrain a comparatively compact target.

We formalize this intuition through the irreducible velocity loss $R_v(t,c)$ of standard Flow Matching, which becomes much smaller toward the noise endpoint for VLA, whereas image-generation models usually exhibit a U-shaped profile.

The geometry induced by the learned generative map shows the same contrast: the Jacobian of this map with respect to the initial noise has a substantially smaller largest singular value for action generation than for image generation.

Together, these results suggest that VLA's condition-target structure makes one-step generation unusually accessible to standard Flow Matching. Code and training configurations for this paper are available at https://github.com/bondtesty/let-it-be-simple.

summary.en: The paper studies one-step action generation for vision-language-action models. It reports that biasing the training timestep distribution toward the noise endpoint yields strong policies across several LIBERO benchmarks and real-world robot tasks. For open-source models with different architectures, replacing iterative decoding with one forward pass often achieves comparable benchmark performance. The authors attribute this to observations strongly constraining compact action targets, and support the explanation with analyses of irreducible velocity loss and the learned map’s Jacobian, contrasting VLA with image generation.
summary.zh: 论文研究视觉语言动作模型的一步动作生成，报告称仅将训练时间步分布偏向噪声端点，就能在多个 LIBERO 基准和真实机器人任务上获得较强策略；对不同架构的开源模型，以单次前向计算替代迭代解码，在若干基准上也常能达到相近表现。作者将其归因于视觉语言动作生成中丰富观测约束紧凑动作目标的结构，并以不可约速度损失及生成映射雅可比的分析支持这一解释；文中对比了其与图像生成的差异。

items.title: Let It Be Simple: One-Step Action Generation for Vision-Language-Action Models

sections.text:
Despite recent progress in dexterous reference tracking, existing models focus primarily on single-hand manipulation and a limited range of interactions, leaving the bimanual dexterous behaviors common in real life unaddressed.

The scarcity of contact-rich bimanual manipulation data and the increased complexity of coordinating contacts make developing a generalist bimanual tracker particularly challenging.

Therefore, we present 1) DONIC, the first generalist bimanual tracker jointly trained across operation categories and human-motion sources, together with 2) BiHOI, a multi-view dataset of 1,575 sequences spanning 229 objects and emphasizing sustained bimanual interaction, where reconstructed interactions are retargeted into robot references.

DONIC combines proximal policy optimization with behavioral cloning in a feedback loop that recycles verified successful executions into training demonstrations. An object-centered per-hand reward maintains object-motion feedback while supervising each hand according to its reference contact role.

Clip-Centered Advantages remove reference-dependent advantage offsets while preserving within-trajectory differences. Together, these designs enable one single policy to learn coordinated manipulation across heterogeneous references.

Without finetuning, a single checkpoint achieves 86.79% success on unseen trajectories of training objects and 57.32% on held-out objects, surpassing the state-of-the-art bimanual tracking baselines by 77.36 and 45.73 percentage points.

summary.en: The paper presents DONIC, a generalist bimanual dexterous tracker trained across operation categories and human-motion sources, alongside BiHOI, a multi-view dataset of sustained two-hand interactions retargeted into robot references. DONIC combines proximal policy optimization and behavioral cloning, recycling verified successful executions. Its rewards use object-motion feedback and reference contact roles, while Clip-Centered Advantages address reference-dependent offsets. Without finetuning, one policy performs on unseen trajectories and held-out objects, exceeding the reported bimanual tracking baselines.

sections.text:
World models aim to improve robotic decision making by predicting the consequences of actions. However, in practice, their predictions often become unreliable once the robot encounters states outside the training distribution, limiting their effectiveness at deployment.

We observe that execution itself provides a natural but underutilized signal: after each action, the robot directly observes the true next state, revealing the mismatch between predicted and actual outcomes.

Building on this insight, we propose feedback world model, an inference-time mechanism that closes the loop between prediction and observation at inference time.

Instead of treating the world model as a static open-loop predictor, our method maintains a lightweight feedback state that is updated online to iteratively correct future predictions, compensating for model errors using real-time observations without additional training data or parameter updates.

We show that this process can be interpreted as a latent-space observer and admits convergence guarantees under bounded, asymptotically convergent dynamics residuals and a stable feedback gain.

We further introduce action-aware guidance to better translate corrected predictions into control by emphasizing action-controllable components while suppressing irrelevant variations.

Experiments on LIBERO-Plus, Robomimic, and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate that our method substantially improves both prediction accuracy and policy performance under distribution shift, reducing world model prediction error by up to 76.4%.

The same feedback mechanism improves the predictions of the pretrained foundation model Fast-WAM-Joint without updating its parameters, demonstrating its plug-and-play applicability. These results show that incorporating real-time feedback at inference time provides a simple yet powerful alternative to static world modeling.

summary.en: The paper proposes an inference-time feedback world model that updates a lightweight state from observed outcomes to iteratively correct future predictions, without extra training data or parameter updates. The authors interpret it as a latent-space observer and state convergence guarantees under specified residual and feedback-gain conditions. Action-aware guidance emphasizes controllable components. Experiments on LIBERO-Plus, Robomimic, and real-world manipulation tasks report improved prediction accuracy and policy performance under distribution shift, with prediction error reduced by up to 76.4%.

sections.text:
Robot deployment generates experience that can support policy improvement, but continued reliance on expert corrective actions makes learning difficult to scale across growing fleets. We propose learning from fleet experience: using deployed robots' own executions as a source of supervision for further policy improvement.

We call this paradigm Collective Experience Learning (CEL), in which robots pool execution experience to update a shared policy that returns to the fleet. Following expert-supervised initialization, we realize CEL through failure-guided experience retrieval fine-tuning (FERT).

FERT uses failure contexts to retrieve relevant segments from successful trajectories and prioritizes their recorded actions for supervised updates, without collecting additional expert demonstrations or corrective actions. Operators provide binary episode-outcome labels and environment resets.

A fault-tolerant asynchronous training system (FATS) coordinates robot execution, cloud inference and policy optimization despite local interruptions. Across five real-world manipulation tasks, the resulting policies achieve success rates of 93.3-99.2%, evaluated over 120 trials per task on robots excluded from training data collection.

With collection time per robot held fixed, larger fleets provide more experience and generally improve performance across the evaluated sizes. On multi-stage phone packaging, learning with 96 robots raises success from 79.2% to 98.3%.

These results support CEL as a scalable approach to improving robot policy reliability through experience generated during deployment.

summary.en: The paper proposes Collective Experience Learning (CEL), in which deployed robots pool execution experience to update a shared policy. Its FERT method uses failure contexts to retrieve segments from successful trajectories and prioritizes recorded actions for supervised updates, without new expert demonstrations or corrective actions; operators provide binary outcomes and reset the environment. A fault-tolerant asynchronous system coordinates execution and training. Across five real-world manipulation tasks, reported success rates range from 93.3% to 99.2%; for phone packaging, learning with 96 robots raises success from 79.2% to 98.3%.

sections.text:
The Moon changes gravity, terrain, and soil at once. Learned locomotion has studied reduced gravity on rigid ground and granular terrain mostly at Earth gravity, but not humanoids under both, generalist-controller transfer, or the Earth cost of lunar adaptation.

On a simulated Unitree G1, we train 12 policies with one recipe, varying gravity, terrain geometry, and ground contact (rigid or three-dimensional resistive force theory, 3D RFT), and including Earth-to-Moon fine-tuning and gravity randomization.

We test them at both gravities on rigid ground and 3D RFT, and at their training gravity on three held-out soil models. We also test the frozen SONIC, a released generalist humanoid controller, at both gravities on rigid ground only. Gravity transfer is asymmetric.

Earth-trained policies keep 0.64 to 0.75 survival at the Moon on flat rigid ground, Moon-trained and fine-tuned policies cannot stand at Earth, and SONIC survives at most 0.10 at the Moon. Rough training lifts combined-tile survival from 0.53 to 0.98 at Earth and 0.80 to 0.99 at the Moon.

In 3D RFT, soil training helps on Earth sand, on tiles and for rough-trained policies also on flat sand. On the stiffer lunar soil it helps only flat-trained Earth policies at Earth and changes the survival of Moon-trained policies by at most a few hundredths.

In the sampled rollouts of the held-out soil models, Moon-trained policies keep most of their rigid-ground progress on lunar regolith at the low G1 foot pressure, with per-seed progress ratios of 0.84 to 1.39 apart from one seed with a short rigid reference.

A gravity-randomized policy trained on rough 3D RFT terrain has a seed-mean survival of at least 0.84 at Earth and 0.96 at the Moon on every key test cell up to 20 degrees. Lunar results are simulation predictions conditional on the contact model and soil stiffness.

summary.en: The paper studies transfer of humanoid locomotion controllers across Earth and lunar gravity, terrain, and soil in simulation using a Unitree G1. It trains 12 policies with varying gravity, terrain, and contact models, and also evaluates frozen SONIC on rigid ground. Transfer is asymmetric: Earth-trained policies retain some survival on flat rigid lunar ground, while Moon-trained and fine-tuned policies cannot stand at Earth. Rough-terrain training improves combined-tile survival at both gravities. Soil-training effects vary by ground and stiffness; lunar findings are simulation predictions conditional on the contact model and soil stiffness.
summary.zh: 论文在 Unitree G1 仿真中研究地球训练的人形机器人控制器向月球重力、地形和土壤条件迁移，比较12种策略，并测试冻结的通用控制器 SONIC。结果显示重力迁移不对称：地球训练策略在月球平坦刚性地面仍有一定存活表现，而月球训练或微调策略无法在地球站立；粗糙地形训练改善两种重力下的组合地面表现。土壤训练的作用随地面和土壤刚度而异。作者强调月球结果是基于接触模型和土壤刚度的仿真预测。

sections.text:
This paper studies heterogeneous multi-team collaboration through dynamic robot allocation, where the robots themselves are treated as transferable resources.

Leveraging Hamilton's rule from ecology as an altruistic decision-making mechanism, we propose a multi-team collaborative resource allocation framework with heterogeneous capabilities, transfer costs, and capability-dependent contributions. The resulting general heterogeneous resource assignment problem is combinatorial and is shown to be NP-hard.

To address scalability, we develop a graph neural network policy under centralized training and decentralized execution that approximates the altruistic allocations based on Hamilton's rule. The model operates over the team interaction graph and predicts robot-level transfer decisions and subsequent robot-to-team assignments.

The proposed approach is evaluated in a fire-fighting scenario against exact optimization and multi-step simulations, quantifying allocation quality, decision computation, and fire suppression.

Five paired physical testbed trials with 15 robots compare learned reallocation with fixed team membership; the GNN reaches the modeled fire stopping threshold in all five trials, compared with two for static allocation.

items.title: Learning Altruistic Collaboration in Heterogeneous Multi-Team Systems

sections.text:
Language models are being explored as the interface through which space robots interpret operator commands and select among verified skills.

Running them onboard calls for low-bit compression, and flight use adds requirements that generic post-training quantization leaves implicit: a fixed memory budget and storage format, a static artifact under configuration control, and behavior close to the full-precision model validated on the ground.

We treat compression as a ground-segment step and study QSelect, which composes one static low-bit model from compatible AWQ, GPTQ, and AutoRound checkpoints by assigning each linear module to one quantizer family and scoring every substitution at the final next-token distribution.

The default fidelity mode needs no labels or tuned thresholds and accepts a substitution only when the forward KL divergence from the BF16 reference decreases; an optional target-adapted mode adds answer likelihood on a small labeled set.

On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, and Llama-3.2-3B at 3 and 4 bits, composed models reach lower mean held-out perplexity than every single-family model in all six settings, and the fidelity mode lowers perplexity and KL further.

In a matched scaffold, final-output scoring gives lower held-out KL than representation-similarity scoring in all 12 paired runs. With labels from training or development splits of the evaluated task families, the target-adapted mode raises 3-bit pooled accuracy on the two Llama models by 4.3 and 4.5 points over the best single-family model.

At 3 bits, unquantized embedding and output layers make up 43-46% of the packed artifact. All evaluations use general-domain benchmarks on a ground GPU; space-domain tasks and flight hardware are left to future work.

items.title: Compressing Onboard Language Models for Space Robots under a Behavioral-Fidelity Requirement

sections.text:
We present SpatialDex, a framework that learns 3D-grounded bimanual dexterity from RGB-only human videos through reconstruction-augmented visuomotor pre-training. The central idea is to learn human behavior together with its spatial context.

From each video, we reconstruct the scene geometry and estimate the hand motion, align them at a shared video-level scale using the hand-size prior of 3D hand estimates. We retain the reconstructed geometry as both a policy input and a prediction target.

The policy grounds the token grid of a pre-trained vision-language model in this geometry through gated residual fusion, is trained to predict future scene geometry alongside wrist and finger actions, and generates finger motion conditioned on the predicted trajectories of both wrists.

Pre-trained on 1M human-video clips and fine-tuned with a small number of robot demonstrations, SpatialDex outperforms the state-of-the-art methods by 16.5 points on nine simulated dexterous tasks across two embodiments and by 38.3 points on six real-world bimanual dexterous tasks.

Under a matched comparison, pre-training with reconstructed geometry improves success by 14.2 points over pre-training on hand motion alone.

items.title: Reconstruction-Augmented Visuomotor Pre-Training of 3D-Grounded Bimanual Dexterity from RGB-Only Human Videos

Despite its promise for scaling robot learning, egocentric manipulation data is still scarce today. Collection at scale requires vertically integrating ergonomic hardware with centimeter-precise 3D algorithms, at a precision that has not been publicly demonstrated.

To address this gap, we introduce RoboCap, a 250\,g six-camera dual-IMU hat designed for in-the-wild egocentric data capture, and the Grounded API, a suite of device-agnostic 3D algorithms tuned for RoboCap.

In this report, we demonstrate how hardware, calibration, and 3D algorithms interact to achieve state-of-the-art performance on the public benchmarks: our SLAM across diverse settings and rigs, our depth estimation on egocentric settings, and our hand tracking when adapted to third-party devices.

summary.en: The paper introduces RoboCap, a 250 g hat with six cameras and dual IMUs for egocentric data capture in the wild, together with Grounded API, a device-agnostic suite of 3D algorithms tuned for the platform. The authors report state-of-the-art performance on public benchmarks for SLAM across diverse settings and rigs, depth estimation in egocentric settings, and hand tracking adapted to third-party devices. The abstract gives no benchmark figures.

sections.text:
Trajectory demonstrations show robots how to behave but not why, leaving them to guess which features of the task actually matter. Incorrect guesses produce misaligned internal representations and lead to incorrect robot behaviors.

Because task features are often semantically defined, we argue that natural language is better suited for specifying features rather than relying on demonstrations.

Although existing representation editing methods have proposed using language to specify new features, only allowing additive edits produces feature sets that are often over-specified or too narrowly scoped, especially in sequential editing tasks.

We propose the Flexible Feature Editing Pipeline (FLEX), which uses language models to iteratively refine a robot's internal representation of task features from natural language corrections via three complementary operations: Add missing features, Generalize existing specific features, and Mask irrelevant features.

We evaluate FLEX on 2D navigation scenarios, 7DoF Franka tabletop manipulation tasks, and a real-world study using naturalistic human language corrections and real-robot demonstrations.

Comparisons against single-operation and unscaffolded baselines show that all three operations are necessary in interactive scenarios, and that FLEX achieves consistently higher normalized reward compared to other feature editing approaches while maintaining compact, transferable representations. Project available at https://mit-clear-lab.github.io/FLEX/

summary.en: The paper proposes FLEX, a pipeline that iteratively edits a robot’s task-feature representation using natural-language corrections. Its three operations add missing features, generalize overly specific ones, and mask irrelevant ones. The authors evaluate it in 2D navigation, 7DoF Franka tabletop manipulation, and a real-world study with naturalistic corrections and robot demonstrations. Comparisons report that all three operations are needed in interactive scenarios and that FLEX achieves consistently higher normalized reward than other feature-editing approaches while keeping representations compact and transferable.
summary.zh: 论文提出 FLEX，通过自然语言纠正迭代调整机器人对任务特征的内部表示，包含补充缺失特征、泛化过于具体的特征和屏蔽无关特征三种操作。作者在二维导航、Franka 桌面操作及真实机器人研究中进行评估；比较结果显示，交互场景需要这三种操作，且 FLEX 相比其他特征编辑方法持续获得更高的归一化奖励，同时保持表示紧凑且可迁移。摘要未说明评估结果适用于更广泛场景。

sections.text:
Flow-matching vision-language-action (VLA) models generate an action chunk by iteratively denoising Gaussian noise, but typically execute only a short prefix before replanning with updated observations. Under this receding-horizon paradigm, the unexecuted remainder---the action tail---is discarded, and the next chunk is regenerated from fresh noise.

We show that this discarded tail retains transferable denoising progress: action-tail initialization can match or outperform a native 10-step Gaussian baseline using fewer denoising steps. However, the optimal denoising budget varies substantially across samples, indicating that tail reuse should be adapted to the updated environment.

Based on this observation, we introduce VLA-Rolling, a lightweight inference framework that reuses action tails through three stages: action-tail inheritance, per-action confidence estimation, and confidence-guided refinement through renoising and denoising budget allocation, while the underlying VLA remains frozen.

Across $\pi_{0.5}$, SmolVLA, X-VLA, and MolmoAct2 on LIBERO, MetaWorld, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin 2.0, VLA-Rolling reduces action-chunk inference cost in all 16 model--benchmark pairs, achieving up to a $1.48\times$ speedup, while improving success rate in 14 pairs by up to $15.08$ percentage points.

These results show that action tails are not merely discarded predictions, but reusable intermediate states that enable more efficient and accurate VLA inference. These results demonstrate that the action tail can support the generation of better actions with fewer denoising steps. Our project is available at https://chenbao123ww.github.io/VLA-Rolling/.

summary.en: VLA-Rolling reuses unexecuted action tails from flow-matching vision-language-action models. Its stages inherit the tail, estimate confidence per action, and use confidence to guide renoising, denoising-budget allocation, and refinement while keeping the underlying model frozen. Across four models and four benchmarks, the authors report lower action-chunk inference cost in all 16 model-benchmark pairs, with speedups up to 1.48×. Success rates improve in 14 pairs, by up to 15.08 percentage points.
summary.zh: 论文提出 VLA-Rolling，在视觉语言动作模型保持冻结的情况下，继承未执行的动作尾部，估计逐动作置信度，并据此重新加噪、分配去噪预算和细化动作。作者在四种模型与四个基准的 16 组组合中报告推理成本均下降，最高加速 1.48 倍；其中 14 组成功率提高，最高增加 15.08 个百分点。这些结果来自摘要所列模型和基准，不能据此推断其他设置的表现。

sections.text:
Learning inertial odometry for a new platform usually requires ground-truth trajectories. We show that an inertial odometry model can instead be trained from scratch by a myopic teacher that integrates the IMU over each short window independently, a scheme we call integration self-supervision.

Interestingly, although supervised only by short-window velocity changes, the student learns to directly predict velocity, and does so more accurately than its integration teacher. Pose graph distillation then refines the model with sequence-consistent targets from a pose graph over many windows.

Training on a new platform therefore no longer requires collecting ground-truth trajectories, but only calibrating the IMU and recording data during normal operation.

Across six datasets spanning pedestrians, drones, quadrupeds, and a humanoid, the same recipe with no velocity or position labels trains models that come within 0.07~m/s average velocity error of a same-architecture supervised baseline.

summary.en: The paper presents self-supervised inertial odometry training using a myopic teacher that independently integrates IMU data over short windows. A student learns velocity prediction from these window-level changes and is then refined through pose-graph distillation across many windows. The authors report that the student predicts velocity more accurately than its integration teacher. The approach uses no velocity or position labels, requiring IMU calibration and data recorded during normal operation. On six datasets spanning pedestrians, drones, quadrupeds, and a humanoid, its average velocity error comes within 0.07 m/s of a same-architecture supervised baseline.

sections.text:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models have achieved strong performance in embodied manipulation, but still struggle to distinguish between changes that should preserve behavior and those that require different actions. We identify two complementary failure modes.

Under task-preserving changes, where task semantics remain unchanged but scene appearance varies (e.g., style, illumination, clutter, or paraphrasing), policies often exhibit unnecessary action drift.

Conversely, under semantic-breaking changes, where key task semantics such as the target object or constraint are altered, policies frequently continue following the original trajectory instead of adapting to the new task. To address these failures, we propose BAS-VLA, a task-semantic action calibration framework built on top of a frozen base VLA.

BAS-VLA adopts a breaking-centered calibration core as its default path, complemented by a selective evidence-gated preserving auxiliary that corrects appearance-induced drift when task-preserving evidence is strong.

Across four target-object swap tasks, BAS-VLA improves changed-task success from 2.3% to 68.5% while maintaining strong clean and semantics-preserving performance and suppressing outdated behavior. On validated style-preserving shifts, it further improves success from 42% to 70% without degrading clean performance.

These results demonstrate the importance of calibrating VLA policies to remain stable when task semantics are preserved and adapt when task semantics change.

summary.en: The paper identifies two failure modes in vision-language-action models: unnecessary action drift when appearance changes but task meaning is preserved, and failure to adapt when task semantics change. It proposes BAS-VLA, which calibrates a frozen base model, emphasizing semantic changes by default and using an evidence-gated auxiliary path for appearance shifts. The authors report that success on four target-object swap tasks rises from 2.3% to 68.5%, and on validated style-preserving shifts from 42% to 70%, while stating that clean performance is maintained.

Classical robot navigation stacks are reliable but often require re-engineering for each new robot type and site. Learning-based navigation shifts this effort from hand-tuned parameters to data generation and training, where a policy adapts to each new embodiment or facility by fine-tuning in simulation.

Whether policies adapted this way stay reliable on real industrial robots has seen little systematic testing. We study this for NVIDIA's X-Mobility and COMPASS workflow for training learned navigation policies on Idealworks robots.

In simulation, we extend the COMPASS benchmark with two embodiments, the differential-drive iw$\mkern-1.5mu.\mkern-1.5mu$hub and an omnidirectional Humanoid Mobile Platform (HMP), and with a digital twin of the Idealworks R&D center.

For the real world, we fine-tune X-Mobility on data from this digital twin, with and without sim-to-real variants generated by NVIDIA Cosmos, train COMPASS on top of it from scratch in the digital twin, deploy the resulting policies on the iw$\mkern-1.5mu.\mkern-1.5mu$hub's onboard Jetson AGX Xavier, and benchmark them in the Idealworks R&D center against COMPASS trained only on NVIDIA's environments and the existing Idealworks navigation stack on task success, efficiency, safety, smoothness and onboard compute.

Running every static scenario both in a digital-twin replica and in the real facility measures the sim-to-real gap and how far Cosmos-augmented data closes it.

Training in the digital twin with Cosmos sim-to-real augmentation raises the real-world success rate of learned navigation from 65.3% to 91.7% across four scenarios and nearly halves its weighted travel time compared with simulation-only training, bringing it within 8.3 points of the production navigation stack, fully onboard; with an integrated global planner, it also reaches far, occluded goals in every trial.

The authors extend the simulation benchmark with two robot embodiments and a digital twin of the R&D center, then deploy policies trained in the twin to an iw.hub onboard computer for real-facility evaluation. They report that Cosmos-generated sim-to-real augmentation raises learned navigation success from 65.3% to 91.7% across four scenarios and nearly halves weighted travel time. With a global planner, the system reaches distant occluded goals in every trial.

sections.text:
Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) show promising reasoning capabilities, but reliable physical interaction requires planning that accounts for when actions are executable and how they change the world. These preconditions and effects are environment-dependent and often not captured by MLLMs, making adaptation challenging.

Yet existing approaches either require costly environment-specific training or rely on unstructured interaction experience that is difficult to reuse. Therefore, we introduce CausGround, a non-parametric causal interaction grounding framework that distills interaction experience into reusable action-centered causal knowledge.

CausGround identifies action preconditions and effects and organizes them in a factorized world-state representation capturing object attributes and inter-object relations.

At planning time, task-relevant causal dependencies are grounded in current observations to support backward reasoning over preconditions and forward reasoning over effects for action selection and multi-step planning. We evaluate CausGround on simulated high-level planning, interaction reasoning, and real-world robot manipulation.

On adapted VirtualHome and RoboCasa benchmarks, CausGround improves vision-based high-level planning across MLLM backbones, increasing average task success from 24.9% to 53.3% on VirtualHome and closed-loop planning success from 43.0% to 57.0% on RoboCasa.

On SWITCH, average interaction reasoning accuracy increases from 25.8% to 31.9%, indicating improved action selection, recovery, and verification. Moreover, real-world experiments show that CausGround reasons backward from MLLM-interpreted goals to derive executable high-level action sequences for sequential manipulation.

These results demonstrate that reusable action preconditions and effects support long-horizon embodied planning across diverse environments without parameter updates.

summary.en: CausGround is a non-parametric framework that organizes interaction experience as reusable causal knowledge about action preconditions, effects, object attributes, and relations. At planning time, it grounds relevant dependencies in current observations to support backward reasoning about preconditions and forward reasoning about effects. The authors evaluate it in simulated planning and interaction-reasoning benchmarks, as well as real-world robot manipulation. They report improved planning success on adapted VirtualHome and RoboCasa benchmarks and higher reasoning accuracy on SWITCH; real-world experiments demonstrate deriving action sequences from interpreted goals.

sections.text:
Fast and reliable manipulation is crucial for practical robot deployment. Although Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently shown remarkable progress as generalist robot policies, their execution often remains temporally inefficient.

A key source of this inefficiency is that policies learn fine-grained temporal patterns from teleoperated demonstrations, requiring many low-level action steps. Temporal action quantization offers a simple way to accelerate execution by aggregating consecutive low-level actions into temporally coarser actions.

However, applying action quantization without considering when fine-grained control is required introduces a speed-accuracy trade-off: accelerated actions may efficiently reduce redundant steps in some phases, while discarding critical motion details in precision-sensitive interactions.

To address this, we propose PaceVLA, a unified framework for adaptive temporal execution in VLAs that integrates two coupled components: （1） mode-specific action decoders built on a shared action expert, supporting multiple temporal granularities and prediction horizons, and （2） a quantizability-guided mode selection scheme which decides whether coarse execution is appropriate, and a context-conditioned router that selects an execution mode at each inference step.

Experiments across three multi-task simulation benchmarks and six real-world tasks show that PaceVLA improves execution efficiency while maintaining task success rate across multiple embodiments, including long-horizon and dexterous manipulation.

summary.en: PaceVLA addresses temporal inefficiency in vision-language-action policies by adaptively quantizing action sequences. It combines mode-specific decoders built on a shared action expert, with multiple temporal granularities and prediction horizons, and a quantizability-guided selection scheme with a context-conditioned router. The framework is intended to use coarser actions when suitable while retaining fine control for precision-sensitive interactions. Experiments across three multi-task simulation benchmarks and six real-world tasks are reported to improve execution efficiency while maintaining task success across embodiments, including long-horizon and dexterous manipulation.
summary.zh: PaceVLA针对视觉-语言-动作模型执行效率不足的问题，提出自适应时间动作量化框架。它包含基于共享动作专家、支持不同时间粒度和预测跨度的模式专用解码器，以及由可量化性引导的模式选择和依据上下文路由执行模式的机制，以便在适合时采用较粗动作，同时保留精细控制。作者报告，在三个多任务仿真基准和六项真实任务中的实验显示，该方法提升执行效率，并在多种机器人形态上维持任务成功率，涵盖长时程和灵巧操作。

Movement primitives commonly represent robot mo- tions through basis functions indexed by time or phase. Inspired by spacetime representations employed in physics, we propose a spline-based formulation in which spatial geometry and temporal progression are represented within a common set of continuous variables.

The proposed method jointly estimates a shared Bezier curve, while allowing spatial and temporal model complexity to be adapted independently (e.g., demonstration-specific phase modulation).As use case, we consider an alternating optimization process that simultaneously estimates path intervals observed in partial demonstrations.

summary.en: This work proposes a spline-based motion representation that describes spatial geometry and temporal progression with shared continuous variables. It jointly estimates a shared Bezier curve while allowing spatial and temporal model complexity to be adjusted independently, including demonstration-specific phase modulation. sections.text:
We present FoveaVLA, a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model that replaces the wrist camera with learned foveation actions. Wrist cameras provide close-up detail but restrict the view to the end-effector's surroundings. External cameras see the whole scene, but the policy receives them at low resolution, so the fine detail needed for manipulation is lost.

FoveaVLA recovers this detail by predicting, alongside each action chunk, the interaction region to observe at the next policy query. The policy then receives crops of these regions, taken from the original-resolution images, together with the full views.

We build FoveaVLA on $\pi_{0.5}$ in two configurations, Single and Dual, using one or two external stereo cameras with full and foveal RGB and depth inputs, and post-train both on DROID with RoboInter interaction annotations.

Across four real-world task suites, FoveaVLA-Single achieves 70.8% success with one external RGB-D view, and FoveaVLA-Dual achieves 77.1%, versus 52.1% for the wrist-equipped $\pi_{0.5}$.Both match the baseline on plain pick-and-place and improve success with distractors, cloth manipulation, and far-away objects.

summary.en: The paper introduces FoveaVLA, which replaces the wrist camera with learned foveation actions. Alongside each action chunk, the model predicts an interaction region for the next policy query, then receives crops from original-resolution images together with full views. The authors build Single and Dual configurations on π0.5 and post-train them on DROID with interaction annotations. Across four real-world task suites, the Single configuration with one external RGB-D view achieves 70.8% success and Dual achieves 77.1%, compared with 52.1% for the wrist-equipped baseline. Both match the baseline on plain pick-and-place and improve results on distractors, cloth manipulation, and distant objects.
summary.zh: 论文提出 FoveaVLA，以学习得到的注视动作取代腕部相机。模型在每个动作块预测下一次查询时要观察的交互区域，并将原始分辨率图像中的局部裁剪与全景视图一同输入。作者基于 π0.5 构建单相机和双相机配置，并使用带交互区域标注的 DROID 数据进行后训练。在四类真实世界任务套件中，单外部 RGB-D 视图配置成功率为 70.8%，双相机配置为 77.1%，腕部相机基线为 52.1%。两种配置在普通抓放任务上与基线相当，在干扰物、布料操作和远处物体任务上成功率更高。

sections.text:
Modern robotic agents are increasingly expected to support steerable control, where a single policy can adjust its behavioral style at runtime under changing user preferences.

Preference-conditioned reinforcement learning provides this interface, but conditioning alone does not ensure that a requested behavior change is strong, does not leak into unrelated behaviors, and does not compromise task performance. Our evaluation combines Preference Reward Responsiveness (PRR) with coverage and utility metrics.

We use these measures to compare reward-level, advantage-level, loss-level, and PCGrad-based aggregation across two humanoid-control frameworks. No aggregation level performs best across all environments and criteria.

Experiments show that aggregating objectives early produces a wider range of behavioral responses but greater unintended changes in other objectives, while aggregating them later improves control precision at some cost to responsiveness.

summary.en: The paper compares where to aggregate objectives in preference-conditioned reinforcement learning for steerable humanoid control. It evaluates whether policies can respond strongly to requested behavior changes, avoid spillover into unrelated behaviors, and maintain task performance. The authors combine Preference Reward Responsiveness with coverage and utility metrics to compare reward-level, advantage-level, loss-level, and PCGrad aggregation across two humanoid-control frameworks. Experiments indicate that no aggregation level performs best across all environments and criteria. Earlier aggregation yields a wider range of behavioral responses but more unintended changes in other objectives; later aggregation improves control precision at some cost to responsiveness.
