sections.text:
Robots deployed in human-centered environments need maps that support both geometric navigation and open-vocabulary semantic queries beyond a fixed label set. A key challenge is enriching such maps with semantic information without relying on manually annotated segmentation masks or closed-set semantic categories.

Existing geometry-driven active mapping maximizes coverage but treats semantics as a passive by-product of the collected trajectory, whereas active semantic mapping typically depends on supervised semantic segmentation. We present AOV-GS, an active 3D Gaussian mapping system that guides exploration using frozen foundation models.

During coarse exploration, AOV-GS re-ranks geometrically promising candidate views according to CLIP mask-embedding novelty computed from SAM instance segmentation, biasing exploration toward semantically informative regions.

Frozen SAM and CLIP provide instance masks and language-aligned embeddings throughout mapping, while a lightweight scene-specific language field is fitted offline directly to the collected CLIP embeddings rather than manually annotated masks, enabling open-vocabulary text-query segmentation on novel views.

In a controlled comparison using the same SAM-CLIP perception stack, AOV-GS improves average language-field mIoU over geometry-only active planning by 1.3 percentage points on Replica (34.6% on eight scenes) and by 1.8 points on Matterport3D (23.1% on five scenes).

With CorrCLIP, AOV-GS reaches 35.6% on Replica, 2.0 points above the matched Geometry-based + CorrCLIP baseline. Novel-view PSNR remains comparable to the geometry-only baseline on both datasets while depth L1 improves on Replica. Code is available at https://github.com/OptimusFaber/AOV-GS.

summary.en: The paper introduces AOV-GS, an active open-vocabulary semantic mapping system using 3D Gaussian mapping with frozen SAM and CLIP models. During coarse exploration, it reranks candidate views using the novelty of CLIP mask embeddings derived from SAM instance segmentation. It fits a scene-specific language field offline from collected CLIP embeddings to support text-query segmentation on novel views. In controlled dataset comparisons, the authors report higher average language-field mIoU than geometry-only planning, comparable novel-view PSNR, and improved depth L1 on Replica.
summary.zh: 本文提出 AOV-GS，一种结合 3D Gaussian 映射与冻结的 SAM、CLIP 模型的主动开放词汇语义建图系统。粗略探索时，它依据 SAM 实例分割得到的 CLIP 掩码嵌入新颖度，对候选视点重新排序；之后直接用收集的 CLIP 嵌入离线拟合场景语言场，以支持新视点上的开放词汇文本查询分割。受控对比显示，在 Replica 和 Matterport3D 数据集上，其语言场平均 mIoU 高于几何规划基线；作者还报告新视点 PSNR 相近，Replica 上深度 L1 有改善。

sections.text:
This paper proposes a refinement to existing vision-based portable pipelines for the recognition of graspable object parts. Such pipelines can effectively support automatic grasp selection and preshaping in upper-limb prosthetic devices. However, realistic scenarios in which multiple objects are present still represent a challenge.

The proposed method exploits a minor modification to the conventional hardware setup and a custom training approach to extend the applicability of vision-based pipelines. A laser pointer is introduced in the setup as an effective mechanism for object disambiguation.

Accordingly, a suitable retraining of the deep convolutional neural networks supporting recognition of graspable parts is implemented. A mixed reality strategy allows the reuse of available high-quality segmentation masks to generate realistic images procedurally, extending the range of scenarios supported by the final device.

Experimental results confirm that the proposed pipeline improves target disambiguation accuracy by up to 9% compared with existing solutions, while preserving the computational cost.

summary.en: The paper proposes a refinement to vision-based recognition of graspable parts for wearable robots in scenes containing multiple objects, supporting automatic grasp selection and preshaping in upper-limb prostheses. It adds a laser pointer for object disambiguation and retrains the deep convolutional networks used to recognize graspable parts. A mixed-reality strategy reuses existing segmentation masks to generate realistic images procedurally. Experiments report up to a 9% improvement in target disambiguation accuracy over existing solutions while preserving computational cost.

sections.text:
Predictive representations for robot manipulation should connect scene geometry with the state changes induced by actions. Our intuition is that understanding what an action will change starts with understanding where things are: complementary RGB and depth observations ground a common scene representation from which to infer those changes.

Guided by this intuition, we introduce \textbf{DepState-JEPA}, a dual-stream RGB--Depth joint-embedding predictive architecture that connects spatial understanding with action-conditioned prediction through a shared latent state, \textbf{DepState}.

Built on V-JEPA~2.1, the framework uses depth both as a complementary observation stream and to ground both modalities in metric 3D space, aggregating shared information into DepState while retaining modality-private features for decoding.

Ray-conditioned readouts predict local features without target depth; after an action-conditioned transition, the same decoders predict future RGB and depth features using the predicted state and fixed initial private features.

Comparisons report stronger results in RGB-encoder transfer, feature completion, conditioned visual forecasting, and manipulation success. items.title: DepState-JEPA: Learning Depth-Grounded State Representation for Visual Perception and Manipulation

Teleoperation enables intuitive control of remote engineering robots for precision tasks. Existing direct joint-mapping methods have two limitations: independent motor saturation disrupts pitch-roll coordination in differential wrists, while fixed mappings struggle with abrupt tracking changes caused by gravitational loads and actuation constraints.

We propose an actuator-constraint-aware leader-follower teleoperation method that jointly models leader gravity compensation, leader-follower joint mapping, and follower differential-wrist control.

Specifically, we perform coordinated saturation in motor space according to the available gravity margin and integrate continuous angle unwrapping, feedback-state monitoring, and feasible-reference updates.

This preserves the operator's motion direction, reduces coordination distortion, and suppresses recovery transients during saturation or brief communication failures. Real-robot experiments demonstrate smoother wrist trajectories and more continuous recovery than direct mapping.

summary.en: The paper proposes actuator-constraint-aware leader-follower teleoperation for manipulators with coupled transmissions. It addresses how independent motor saturation can disrupt pitch-roll coordination in differential wrists and how fixed mappings can struggle with tracking changes caused by gravity and actuation limits. The method jointly models leader gravity compensation, leader-follower joint mapping, and follower wrist control. It coordinates motor-space saturation using available gravity margin and incorporates angle unwrapping, feedback monitoring, and feasible-reference updates. Real-robot experiments report smoother wrist trajectories and more continuous recovery than direct mapping.

sections.text:
Vision-based manipulation policies are commonly learned from rich visual observations, typically using dense visual features extracted from full resolution images. It remains unclear how much of this visual information is really needed for effective policy learning.

In this paper, we investigate the opposite end of the spectrum: how effective can manipulation policies be if they use as input only a compact visual representation. Sparse 2D keypoints provide a deliberately compact representation, giving the policy spatial information while removing direct access to appearance, texture, and background.

We design AFFORD2ACT (Affordance-Guided Keypoints to Act) to study how much manipulation capability can be retained under this representation constraint. An off-the-shelf language-conditioned affordance model identifies the task-relevant region, from which up to 15 object keypoints are selected, together with 4 end-effector keypoints.

The policy input is therefore reduced to only 19 2D keypoints (38 coordinates).A lightweight gating further decides which keypoints to pay attention to during execution.

Across six real-robot manipulation tasks, this compact state outperforms the evaluated RGB, RGB-D, and dense-affordance behavior cloning baselines, degrades less as the number of demonstrations is reduced, and achieves 82% average success in held-out settings. Replacing learned gating with uniform weights reduces success from 92% to 52%.

At the same time, the representation depends on reliable affordance localization and keypoint tracking, and remains vulnerable to incorrect masks, occlusion, tracking drift, and distractors.

summary.en: The paper presents AFFORD2ACT, which studies robot manipulation policies using sparse 2D keypoints instead of dense visual observations. An off-the-shelf language-conditioned affordance model identifies task-relevant regions; up to 15 object keypoints and four end-effector keypoints yield a 38-coordinate input, with learned gating selecting which points to attend to. Across six real-robot tasks, the authors report better performance than evaluated RGB, RGB-D, and dense-affordance behavior-cloning baselines, less degradation with fewer demonstrations, and 82% average success in held-out settings. The approach depends on reliable localization and tracking.

items.title: AFFORD2ACT: How Far Can Sparse Keypoints Go for Robot Manipulation?

sections.text:
Robots must act under physical and social constraints while adapting to changes in their environment and human needs. Existing embodied-agent systems often focus on specified goals or abstract execution into symbolic actions, limiting evaluation in an evolving world.

We introduce TARSphere, a robot-oriented full-stack framework for physically and socially grounded long-horizon embodied agents. TARSphere-Infra runs robot policies in a physics simulator with embodied NPCs and constrained dialogue.

An event-driven finite-state machine (FSM) uses completed actions and delivered information to update task states and evaluate outcomes.

TARSphere-Harness, its embodied brain harness, lets a frozen multimodal large language model (MLLM) act through multi-level executable skills, using observations, hierarchical memory, and execution feedback to revise its decisions.

On this foundation, agent-in-the-loop curation aligns task semantics, causal dependencies, and scene geometry to construct TARSphere-Bench: 360 episodes across 30 indoor scenes.

Five paired conditions assess perceptual robustness, disruption adaptation, task update, human coordination, and intent understanding for navigate-and-report and fetch-and-deliver tasks. Our evaluation of 8 MLLMs shows that general-purpose models can outperform embodied models, while task updates and human interaction remain difficult.

Frequent collisions and falls further motivate evaluating execution safety alongside task success, even with a shared action interface and decision budget.

summary.en: The paper introduces TARSphere, a full-stack framework for long-horizon embodied agents grounded in physical and social environments. Its infrastructure runs robot policies in a physics simulator with embodied NPCs and constrained dialogue; an event-driven state machine updates tasks based on completed actions and delivered information. A harness lets a frozen multimodal language model act through executable skills and revise decisions using observations, hierarchical memory, and execution feedback. The benchmark contains 360 episodes across 30 indoor scenes. Evaluation of eight models finds general-purpose models can outperform embodied models, while task updates and human interaction remain difficult; collisions and falls motivate assessing execution safety.
summary.zh: 论文提出 TARSphere，一个面向长时程具身智能体的机器人全栈框架。其基础设施在物理模拟器中运行机器人策略，并包含具身 NPC 和受约束对话；事件驱动有限状态机依据已完成动作与已传递信息更新任务状态。具身脑部组件使冻结的多模态大语言模型通过多层级可执行技能行动，并利用观察、分层记忆和执行反馈修正决策。基准包含30个室内场景的360个片段，评估感知鲁棒性、适应干扰、任务更新、人类协作和意图理解。对8个模型的评估显示，通用模型可胜过具身模型，但任务更新和人际互动仍困难，碰撞与跌倒也提示需评估执行安全。

items.title: TARSphere: A Robot-Oriented Full-Stack Framework for Long-Horizon Embodied Agents in Evolving Physical and Social Environments

sections.text:
During steady pouring, images and robot pose may remain nearly unchanged while transferred mass accumulates, making the return decision ambiguous for a whole-task vision-language-action (VLA) policy. We present FlowVLA, which separates motor generation from physical-completion estimation.

A shared $\pi_{0.5}$ action expert learns approach, pour, and return with boundary-aware supervision. A target-independent estimator fuses visual, joint, wrist-wrench, and recurrent force-belief histories to maintain an estimate of transferred mass. The controller initiates return when this estimate plus predicted residual outflow reaches the requested mass.

In coffee-pot/water experiments, FlowVLA achieves 13.1 g goal-balanced mean absolute error (MacroMAE), lower than all tested VLA baselines. Across all attempts, 53.7% both complete the task and finish within +/-10% of the requested mass. The same model interpolates to held-out 150/250-g targets without retraining.

Independently trained models further evaluate the formulation in three additional container-fluid settings.

summary.en: FlowVLA separates action generation from estimating physical task completion. A shared action expert learns approach, pouring, and return, while an estimator combines visual, joint, wrist-wrench, and recurrent force-belief histories to estimate transferred mass. The controller returns when estimated mass plus predicted residual outflow reaches the requested amount. In coffee-pot and water experiments, the authors report lower goal-balanced mean absolute error than all tested VLA baselines; 53.7% of attempts both completed the task and ended within ±10% of the requested mass. The model interpolated to held-out targets without retraining, and independently trained models were evaluated in three additional container-fluid settings.
summary.zh: 论文提出 FlowVLA，将动作生成与物理完成度估计分开：共享动作专家学习接近、倾倒和返回，估计器融合视觉、关节、腕部力觉及历史力信念来估算转移质量，并结合预测的残余流量决定何时返回。在咖啡壶向水实验中，作者报告其目标均衡平均绝对误差低于测试的 VLA 基线；53.7% 的尝试既完成任务又达到请求质量的 ±10% 范围。模型还可在不重新训练的情况下插值到留出的 150 克和 250 克目标。另以独立训练模型在三种容器与流体设置中评估该方法。

items.title: FlowVLA: Learning Flow-Aware Physical Completion for Quantitative Robotic Pouring

sections.text:
LEGO walkers are walking automata constructed from modular LEGO Technic bricks. They exhibit intriguing locomotion and are also highly reconfigurable through the modular Technic bricks, making them widely applicable in education, recreation, and robotics research.

However, existing LEGO walkers are designed mostly by reusing existing single-actuator walking mechanisms. Although the locomotion is stable, their fixed walking gaits limit their adaptability and versatility.

This paper presents the first computational solution capable of designing LEGO walkers that not only walk stably, but also support a variety of walking gaits. Our idea is twofold.

First, we control the foot motion trajectory of each leg mechanically via a specifically-designed gear-linkage mechanism, in which we incorporate a pair of 3D-printed non-circular gears to work with a LEGO Technic mechanism.

Second, we drive each leg by an independent motor and synchronize the timings of multiple leg motions via a simple yet adaptable control algorithm, enabling stable and versatile locomotion. Importantly, we take this modeling as a foundation to co-design the morphology and control of the LEGO walkers to meet the target locomotion and appearance.

Leveraging our approach, we created a variety of LEGO walkers, demonstrating various walking gaits and appearances, and fabricated some of them to show their locomotion capability in the real world.

summary.en: The paper presents a computational method for designing LEGO walkers with stable, varied gaits. A gear-linkage mechanism, incorporating 3D-printed non-circular gears with LEGO Technic components, mechanically controls each leg’s foot trajectory. Independent motors drive the legs, and an adaptable algorithm synchronizes their motion. The authors also co-design morphology and control to meet target locomotion and appearance. They created walkers with different gaits and looks, and fabricated some to demonstrate locomotion in the real world.
summary.zh: 论文提出一种用于计算设计 LEGO 步行机器人的方法，目标是实现稳定且多样的步态。每条腿的足部轨迹由专门设计的齿轮连杆机构控制，其中非圆齿轮与 LEGO Technic 机构配合；各腿由独立电机驱动，并通过控制算法同步运动时序。作者进一步将形态与控制共同设计，以满足目标运动和外观。研究制作了多种步态与外观的机器人，并实际制造其中一些，以展示其现实环境中的运动能力。

items.title: Make it Walk: Computational Design of LEGO Walkers

sections.text:
Real-time whole-body humanoid teleoperation remains challenging due to the computational latency introduced by optimization-based retargeting pipelines and future-frame conditioning.

Existing motion tracking policies typically require dense reference targets including full joint positions, body-part transformations, and even future frames, which tightly couples the controller to expensive upstream modules.

In this work, we present HuMiT, a whole-body teleoperation system built on a unified tracking policy that requires only a compact reference target, consisting of root height, root velocity, and the SE（3） poses of four sparse keypoints at the current frame, yet achieves competitive tracking fidelity compared to methods relying on more diverse reference states including complete joint positions, dense body-part transformations, and even future frames.

Experiments show that our policy achieves a communication-to-inference latency of $\sim$20 ms measured between headset streaming and policy output and a video-based optical flow latency of 65 ms (median) across different motion types.

We validate the system on a Unitree G1 humanoid, showcasing split-second reactive responses such as catching a tossed ball, as well as coordinated loco-manipulation capabilities. Project page: https://xiaohu-art.github.io/Track/.

summary.en: HuMiT is a whole-body humanoid teleoperation system built around a unified tracking policy. It uses a compact current-frame reference: root height, root velocity, and the SE(3) poses of four sparse keypoints. The authors report tracking fidelity competitive with methods that use richer reference states. Experiments measured about 20 ms communication-to-inference latency from headset streaming to policy output and a median video-based optical-flow latency of 65 ms. Validation on a Unitree G1 humanoid demonstrated rapid reactions, including catching a tossed ball, and coordinated loco-manipulation.
summary.zh: 论文提出 HuMiT，一种基于统一跟踪策略的全身人形机器人遥操作系统。它只需当前帧的紧凑参考目标，包括根部高度、根部速度和四个稀疏关键点的 SE（3）位姿；作者称其跟踪效果可与使用更丰富参考状态的方法相比。实验报告头显数据流至策略输出的通信到推理延迟约为 20 毫秒，基于视频的光流延迟中位数为 65 毫秒。系统在 Unitree G1 人形机器人上验证，展示了接抛球的快速反应及协调的移动操作能力。

items.title: HuMiT: Low-Latency Whole-Body Humanoid Teleoperation via Compact Reference Tracking

sections.text:
A mobile robot following a graph of known routes can make costly navigation errors when a temporary obstacle blocks a critical edge: waiting too long behind a parked cart wastes time, but immediately rerouting around a person who would move in a few seconds is also inefficient.

Standard reactive obstacle avoidance addresses local motion around obstacles, while fixed wait-or-reroute rules ignore how long different obstacle types tend to persist. We propose OSCAR: an adaptive survival-modeling framework for graph-based navigation with temporary blockages.

Assuming obstacle class labels are available at encounter time, the robot learns class-conditioned residual clearance-time distributions from online experience, including right-censored observations when it reroutes before observing clearance.

These survival models are integrated into a time-dependent graph planner that maintains obstacle memory and computes a patience threshold at each blocked edge: how long to wait before taking an alternate route. The method continuously updates its clearance estimates across episodes and uses them to balance waiting against rerouting.

We evaluate the approach in simulation and on a real mobile robot in a university atrium with obstacles including people, chairs, bins, and tubes.

In simulation, the learned policy's time-to-goal converges to within 1% of an oracle with access to ground-truth clearance distributions after fewer than 20 observations per obstacle class, outperforming all heuristic baselines.

Real-world deployment confirms that the policy improves online, adapting its patience thresholds from experience across 50 navigation episodes.

summary.en: The paper presents OSCAR for graph-based navigation with temporary blockages. Assuming obstacle class labels are available, it learns class-conditioned residual clearance-time distributions from online experience, including censored observations when the robot reroutes before clearance. A time-dependent planner uses these estimates to choose how long to wait at a blocked edge. In simulation, after fewer than 20 observations per class, time-to-goal converges to within 1% of an oracle with ground-truth distributions and beats heuristic baselines. A real-robot deployment in a university atrium across 50 episodes demonstrates online adaptation.
summary.zh: 论文提出 OSCAR，用于图路线导航中应对暂时性障碍。假设机器人遇到障碍时能获得类别标签，方法根据在线经验学习各类别剩余清除时间的分布，并纳入计及时间的图规划器，计算在受阻边等待多久再改道；若改道前障碍尚未清除，也利用删失观测。仿真中，少于每类20次观测后，策略的到达目标时间收敛至拥有真实清除分布信息的预言机的1%以内，并优于启发式基线。大学中庭的真实机器人部署覆盖50次导航，摘要称策略能在线调整耐心阈值。

items.title: OSCAR: Obstacle Survival Curves for Adaptive Robot Navigation

sections.text:
Recursive self-improvement (RSI) describes a system that improves not only its behavior but also the process by which it improves. Recent digital agents test this idea by rewriting their own code and checking each version with executable tests.

Bringing these mechanisms into the physical world requires learning from partial observations through costly trials, while accounting for changing operating conditions and potentially irreversible consequences. We position RSI within robot learning and trace pathways from improving robot capabilities to improving the processes that generate them.

We examine how physical experience can strengthen these improvement mechanisms and when the resulting gains can support further self-improvement of the mechanisms themselves.

Gains carry forward only when feedback addresses remaining learning needs, the receiving component can use the change, its value survives changes in tasks or hardware, and continued practice remains safe and affordable. Existing studies, concentrated in manipulation, support behavioral improvement, benefits to later learning, and procedure improvement.

Some systems also change the improver's knowledge or tools, but the physical studies reviewed here have yet to isolate gains attributable to recursion. We synthesize these findings into evaluation principles and research directions for machines that, trial by trial, safely improve the way they improve.

summary.en: This paper examines recursive self-improvement (RSI) in physical AI, where robots learn from partial observations and costly trials amid changing conditions and potentially irreversible consequences. It traces routes from improving robot behavior to improving the processes that produce it. The authors argue that gains persist only when feedback addresses remaining learning needs, components can use changes, benefits transfer across task or hardware changes, and practice remains safe and affordable. Reviewed studies, mostly in manipulation, support behavioral, later-learning, and procedural improvements, but have not isolated gains attributable to recursion.
summary.zh: 论文讨论如何将递归自我改进（RSI）从数字智能体扩展到物理机器人：机器人需从有限观察和昂贵试验中学习，并面对环境变化及可能不可逆的后果。作者梳理行为能力提升与改进过程本身提升的路径，并指出经验收益能否延续，取决于反馈是否满足后续学习需求、接收组件能否利用改动，以及收益在任务或硬件变化后是否保留，同时练习须安全且可负担。作者综述称，现有研究主要集中于操作任务，支持行为、后续学习和程序的改进，但尚未分离出递归本身带来的收益。

sections.text:
Vision-language-action (VLA) navigation models translate visual observations and instructions into actions. Navigation success assesses whether an agent reaches the goal. However, reaching the goal successfully does not establish whether the model genuinely follows the instructions or relies on visual cues or navigation history.

We introduce NavBind to diagnose instruction-action binding: whether changing the instruction influences the probabilistic distribution of the actions, with the navigation context fixed. We construct 3,252 route-fork contexts by recombining route-aligned instruction segments from R2R-CE and RxR-CE.

Each context pairs full instructions that share the description of the route already traveled but specify different branches. Both are evaluated under the same agent state and navigation history.

We compare generated local action sequences, the likelihoods of fixed reference action sequences under both instructions, and changes in visual attention and attribution. Across the evaluated models, higher reported navigation success does not imply that the model more faithfully follows the instructions.

summary.en: The paper introduces NavBind to assess whether navigation vision-language-action models change their action distributions when instructions change while context remains fixed. It constructs 3,252 route-fork contexts from R2R-CE and RxR-CE, pairing instructions that describe the traveled route but specify different branches. Both instructions are evaluated with the same agent state and history. The study compares generated local actions, likelihoods of reference action sequences, and changes in visual attention and attribution. The authors report that higher navigation success among evaluated models does not imply more faithful instruction following.

sections.text:
Building a low-latency humanoid teleoperation system is essential for collecting diverse reactive and dynamic demonstrations. However, end-to-end latencies in existing approaches consistently hover around 200ms, roughly equal to human reaction time, that severely limits responsiveness and prevents tasks requiring rapid feedback.

We identify position-only PD control as the root cause of this latency floor and propose ExtremControl, a low-latency whole-body control framework that: （1） incorporates scaled velocity feedforward in low-level control, reducing tracking delay by approximately 70ms with a provably optimal feedforward ratio; （2） operates directly on SE（3） poses of selected rigid links, primarily humanoid extremities, to avoid joint-space retargeting in the control loop.

To minimize retargeting time, we derive a closed-form Cartesian-space mapping that uses a single anthropomorphic calibration step to translate human motion into humanoid link targets, accommodating operators with varying body proportions.

Furthermore, we provide a theoretical framework for selecting control hyperparameters, and validate the effectiveness of velocity feedforward control in the reinforcement learning for locomotion setting through experiments in both simulation and the real world.

Building on ExtremControl, we implement a teleoperation system supporting both optical motion capture and VR-based tracking, achieving end-to-end latency as low as 50ms --- well beneath the threshold at which system delay adds a full human reaction cycle to the control loop.

This enables a qualitatively new class of reactive behaviors, including ping-pong ball balancing, juggling, and real-time return, that are beyond the capability of existing teleoperation systems.

summary.en: The paper presents ExtremControl, a whole-body control framework for humanoid teleoperation. It addresses what the authors identify as a latency floor from position-only PD control by adding scaled velocity feedforward at the low level and directly controlling SE(3) poses of selected rigid links, avoiding joint-space retargeting in the control loop. The authors also describe a one-step anthropomorphic calibration mapping and a framework for choosing control hyperparameters. They report validation of velocity feedforward in locomotion reinforcement-learning experiments in simulation and the real world. A system using optical motion capture and VR tracking reaches an end-to-end latency as low as 50 ms and supports behaviors including ping-pong balancing, juggling, and real-time returns.

sections.text:
World models that capture how actions induce physical change enable scalable robot learning without reliance on embodiment-specific action labels. Pixel-space video models provide broad visual priors but expend model capacity on dense appearance reconstruction, while direct action models require embodiment-specific labels that hinder scalability.

We present $\mu_0$, a scalable world model based on 3D traces. Rather than predicting dense pixels or directly modeling actions, $\mu_0$ forecasts smooth 3D trajectories for salient interaction points such as objects, tools, hands, and contact regions, yielding a compact, embodiment-agnostic motion interface.

To enable training from diverse video sources, our TraceExtract system automatically extracts 3D supervision by selecting keypoints, constructing globally aligned traces, and associating motion segments with hierarchical language captions.

This TraceExtract supervision pretrains $\mu_0$ by combining a pretrained vision-language backbone with a modular trace expert, which represents each query via B-spline control points and predicts future traces. Experiments show that $\mu_0$ outperforms baselines in both 2D and 3D trace prediction, including trace prediction models and tokenized VLM methods.

Because $\mu_0$ is frozen and reusable, it can be paired with action experts for downstream robot embodiments. Despite action-free pretraining, the resulting trace-conditioned policies achieve performance competitive with VLA models pretrained with action supervision, such as $\pi_0$.

These results establish 3D traces as a scalable and transferable representation for cross-embodiment manipulation.

summary.en: The paper presents μ₀, a scalable world model based on 3D interaction traces. It predicts smooth trajectories for salient points such as objects, tools, hands, and contact regions, providing a compact motion interface that does not depend on a specific embodiment. TraceExtract automatically derives 3D supervision from diverse videos and associates motion segments with hierarchical language captions. The model combines a pretrained vision-language backbone with a trace expert. Experiments reported by the authors show better 2D and 3D trace prediction than baselines. When paired with action experts, the frozen model supports trace-conditioned policies that the authors say perform competitively with VLA models pretrained using action supervision.
summary.zh: 论文提出 μ₀，一种基于 3D 交互轨迹的可扩展世界模型，预测物体、工具、手和接触区域等显著交互点的平滑轨迹，作为紧凑且不依赖具体具身形式的运动接口。TraceExtract 自动从多样视频中提取 3D 监督信号，并关联分层语言描述；模型结合预训练视觉语言骨干网络与轨迹专家进行训练。实验中，作者报告 μ₀ 在 2D 和 3D 轨迹预测上优于基线。冻结后的模型可与动作专家配合；论文称，尽管预训练不使用动作标签，轨迹条件策略仍达到与使用动作监督预训练的 VLA 模型相竞争的表现。

items.title: $\mu_0$: A Scalable 3D Interaction-Trace World Model

sections.text:
Physical AI aims to build embodied agents that perceive the world, understand and reason about it, and decide how to act. Yet the field has focused primarily on the last component: the action model that maps observations to low-level controls.

The prevailing training recipe can erode the perceptual and reasoning capabilities needed for robust behavior, leaving even strong action models vulnerable to scene perturbations and long-horizon tasks.

We introduce HarnessPAI, a model- and embodiment-agnostic Harness framework for Physical AI that treats code as the executable and evolvable interface that organizes the underlying action primitive.

The framework separates two timescales: within a rollout, it executes open-loop at the program level, with a fixed program guiding and checking execution; across rollouts, it evolves closed-loop, using execution feedback to revise the program and distill failures into reusable skills.

Across desktop robot arms, household robots, a robot vacuum, and a legged walking agent, HarnessPAI demonstrates consistent improvements against baselines.

Beyond the harness, the converged program also acts as a low-cost, reliable source of expert data: it generates training data for fine-tuning VLA and WAM models on tasks where it is hard for these models to obtain successful trajectories on their own.

Our results suggest that the frontier of Physical AI depends not only on stronger action models, but also on executable harnesses that integrate perception, task understanding and reasoning, and action execution into a unified, verifiable, and feedback-driven system. Website: https://darwin-agent.github.io/HarnessPAI

summary.en: The paper introduces HarnessPAI, a model- and embodiment-agnostic framework for Physical AI that treats code as an executable, evolvable interface for organizing action primitives. Within a rollout, a fixed program guides and checks execution open-loop; across rollouts, execution feedback is used to revise the program and distill failures into reusable skills. The authors report improvements over baselines across desktop robot arms, household robots, a robot vacuum, and a legged walking agent. They also describe using converged programs to generate expert data for fine-tuning VLA and WAM models on tasks where those models struggle to obtain successful trajectories independently.
summary.zh: 论文提出 HarnessPAI，一个与模型和具身形式无关的 Physical AI 框架，把代码作为组织底层动作原语的可执行、可演进接口。框架将执行分为两个时间尺度：单次 rollout 内由固定程序以开环方式引导并检查执行；不同 rollout 之间则依据执行反馈修订程序，并将失败经验提炼为可复用技能。作者报告，该框架在桌面机械臂、家用机器人、扫地机器人和腿式行走智能体上，相较基线均有改进。收敛后的程序还可生成专家数据，用于微调难以自行获得成功轨迹的 VLA 和 WAM 模型。

items.title: HarnessPAI: An Evolving Harness for Physical AI

sections.text:
Multimodal agents (MMAs) sustain interaction through reasoning, memory, tools, and feedback, most visibly as computer-use agents, while robotic systems (RSs) couple sensing and actuation under physical dynamics.

We define multimodal embodied agents (MMEAs) as goal-directed systems that couple multimodal task reasoning with physical action and revise decisions from the resulting feedback. This raises a central question: what changes when a multimodal agent moves from computer-use to robot-use?

We introduce PAPAV, a unified capability-centric framework of five recurring functions: Perceive the current state, Anticipate action effects, Plan a feasible course, Act through an interface or body, and Verify the outcome.

Defined by function rather than architecture, these capabilities let PAPAV identify what all three share and then compare MMEAs with MMAs and with RSs. Five physical constraints, from partial observability to unverifiable outcomes, leave fewer choices fixed in advance and less room to reverse errors.

Across 64 benchmarks, explicit evaluation centers on Act; only 5 assess Anticipate and 3 assess Verify, leaving both largely hidden behind task success. These constraints also frame the open challenges we identify.

PAPAV therefore provides a common basis for designing reliable physical agents and measuring progress across all five capabilities rather than task success alone.

summary.en: The paper defines multimodal embodied agents as goal-directed systems that combine multimodal reasoning with physical action and revise decisions using feedback. It introduces PAPAV, a capability framework covering Perceive, Anticipate, Plan, Act, and Verify, to compare these agents with multimodal agents and robotic systems. The authors report that, among 64 benchmarks, evaluation focuses mainly on Act; five assess Anticipate and three assess Verify. They argue that physical constraints make these capabilities important to evaluate beyond task success.
summary.zh: 本文提出多模态具身智能体（MMEA）的定义及能力框架 PAPAV，用感知、预判、规划、行动和验证五项功能，比较多模态智能体、具身智能体与机器人系统。作者指出，物理环境中的部分可观测性等约束减少了预先固定的选择，也使错误更难逆转。对64项基准的分析显示，评估多集中于行动，只有5项评估预判、3项评估验证。作者据此提出，应围绕五项能力衡量进展，而不只看任务成功。

items.title: Multimodal Embodied Agents: A Unified Capability-centric Perspective from Computer-Use to Robot-Use

To automatically determine intervention timing and recovery strategies, we develop an Agent-Compiled Progress Graph that tracks task progress using privileged simulator state and retains stable

sections.text:
Human-in-the-loop (HIL) post-training improves vision-language-action (VLA) policies through expert corrections, but costly human supervision and repeated real-robot evaluation limit algorithm exploration and development.

We introduce SimPT (Simulation-based Post-Training), a simulation framework that automates intervention-based VLA post-training by integrating policy rollouts, corrective data collection, policy training, and standalone evaluation.

To automatically determine intervention timing and recovery strategies, we develop an Agent-Compiled Progress Graph that tracks task progress using privileged simulator state and retains stable snapshots during policy execution.

After a rollout fails, a CuRobo-based expert attempts recovery from these snapshots, starting at more advanced task stages and falling back to earlier ones as needed to generate corrective trajectories. We implement and compare four post-training methods, RECAP, HG-DAgger, DPO+SFT, and FlowPRO, across seven RoboTwin manipulation tasks.

Relative to a fixed-interval snapshot baseline, the Progress Graph reduces recovery attempts by 75.0% and increases recovery success from 93.4% to 98.9%.Using SimPT, we develop RECAP-CF-LPF, a refinement of RECAP that combines cross-fitting and low-pass filtering of value predictions.

This refinement increases the overall success rate from 76.50% to 79.36% in held-out simulation trials. In real-robot HIL post-training, it increases the success rate from 72% to 96% across 25 scenarios of an Ethernet cable-insertion task. These results demonstrate the utility of SimPT for exploring and developing VLA post-training algorithms.

summary.en: The paper presents SimPT, a simulation framework for intervention-based VLA post-training that combines policy rollouts, corrective data collection, training, and standalone evaluation. Its Progress Graph tracks task progress using privileged simulator state and saves stable snapshots. After a failed rollout, a CuRobo-based expert attempts recovery from later stages before falling back as needed. Across seven RoboTwin tasks, the authors compare four methods. Against a fixed-interval snapshot baseline, the graph reduces recovery attempts and raises recovery success. RECAP-CF-LPF also improves success in held-out simulation trials and real-robot cable-insertion scenarios.
summary.zh: 本文介绍 SimPT，这是一个用于干预式视觉—语言—动作策略后训练的仿真框架，整合策略运行、纠正数据收集、训练和独立评估。其进度图利用特权仿真状态跟踪任务进展并保存快照；运行失败后，CuRobo 专家尝试从较后阶段开始恢复，再按需回退。作者在七项 RoboTwin 操作任务中比较四种后训练方法。相较固定间隔快照基线，进度图减少恢复尝试并提高恢复成功率。RECAP-CF-LPF 在留出仿真试验和真实机器人以太网线插入任务中取得更高成功率；作者认为这些结果显示 SimPT 有助于探索后训练算法。

items.title: SimPT: An Automated Simulation Framework for Intervention-Based VLA Post-Training

sections.text:
Humanoid loco-manipulation requires coordinated whole-body interaction with the physical world, yet collecting robot demonstrations at scale remains costly.

Human demonstrations offer a scalable alternative, but existing egocentric human supervision often omits locomotion and posture, while embodiment differences and controller dynamics hinder accurate end-effector execution.

We introduce HumanVerse, a 500-hour dataset of open-world human loco-manipulation pairing egocentric video with synchronized body and hand motion. Our human-to-humanoid pipeline aligns camera viewpoints and arm appearance, and refines motion references and controller inputs offline to reduce end-effector errors while preserving whole-body coordination.

We validate the pipeline through zero-shot transfer to Unitree G1 on representative whole-body manipulation and long-range loco-manipulation tasks, without target-task robot demonstrations.

Building on this pipeline, we develop $\lambda_0$, a humanoid foundation model for whole-body loco-manipulation, with robot-aligned human demonstrations providing supervision for mid-training.

Increasing whole-body human data consistently improves downstream task progress. $\lambda_0$ achieves 90.0% success on SIMPLE and 62.5% across real-world loco-manipulation tasks. We expect this study to guide scalable whole-body human data collection toward humanoid foundation models for richer interaction with the physical world.

Homepage: https://lambdahumanoid.github.io/

summary.en: The paper introduces HumanVerse, a 500-hour dataset pairing egocentric video with synchronized body and hand motion for open-world human loco-manipulation. Its human-to-humanoid pipeline aligns camera viewpoints and arm appearance, then refines motion references and controller inputs offline to reduce end-effector errors while retaining whole-body coordination. The authors report zero-shot transfer to Unitree G1 on representative manipulation and long-range tasks without target-task robot demonstrations. They develop λ₀, a whole-body loco-manipulation foundation model, and report that more whole-body human data improves downstream progress, with results on SIMPLE and real-world tasks.
summary.zh: 本文提出 HumanVerse，一个包含500小时开放环境人类全身移动与操作数据集，将第一人称视频与同步身体和手部动作配对。作者构建人类到人形机器人的迁移流程，通过对齐视角和手臂外观，并离线修正动作参考与控制器输入，减少末端执行误差，同时保留全身协调。该流程在没有目标任务机器人示范的情况下，迁移至 Unitree G1 的代表性全身操作及远距离移动操作任务。基于此，作者开发人形全身移动操作基础模型 λ₀，并报告增加全身人类数据可持续提升下游任务进展；其在 SIMPLE 和真实世界任务上取得所述成功率。

Retargeting human motion to humanoids requires preserving motion semantics while accounting for the robot's physical constraints. Kinematic pipelines prescribe a robot trajectory through geometric matching, without establishing whether it can be executed under the robot's dynamics.

Prior physics-supervised neural methods train bidirectional full-sequence models on physics-refined kinematic trajectories, remaining tied to prescribed kinematic solutions and requiring noncausal context. We propose SMR, a streaming neural motion retargeter learned from semantic-conditioned physics experts.

We convert human motion into robot-aware task-space targets for body landmark positions, orientations, and velocities. Physics experts track these targets directly in simulation under contact, dynamics, and actuator constraints.

We train a single strictly causal Transformer on their executed state trajectories that complete the motion and pass semantic and physical validity checks. At each incoming frame, the student uses only current and past human observations to generate a robot motion reference for a downstream whole-body controller.

Experiments demonstrate that semantic-conditioned physics experts generate motion with higher semantic fidelity and physical validity than direct optimization-based retargeting, while the resulting streaming retargeter achieves improved closed-loop performance over kinematic and physics-refined baselines under a common whole-body controller.

summary.en: The paper introduces SMR, a streaming neural motion retargeter learned from semantic-conditioned physics experts. Human motion is converted into robot-aware task-space targets, which experts track in simulation under contact, dynamics, and actuator constraints. A strictly causal Transformer is trained on the experts’ executed trajectories and generates robot motion references from current and past human observations. Experiments report higher semantic fidelity and physical validity for the experts than direct optimization-based retargeting, and improved closed-loop performance over kinematic and physics-refined baselines under a common whole-body controller.

sections.text:
Snake robots can traverse complex environments with limbless locomotion, but maneuvering in low-clearance environments remains challenging because a gait must maintain a small swept height while also providing planar steering.

Existing rolling gaits preserve a low swept height body configuration but generally provide limited steering, whereas steering gaits often introduce vertical undulation and require additional clearance.

With that in mind, this paper develops S-rolling, a steerable rolling gait that combines low swept height locomotion with planar maneuverability for twistable snake robots. S-rolling is designed using an S-shaped planar backbone curve, whose head and tail segments roll with independently controlled angular velocities, producing different motion modes.

We derive its joint space gait equation, in which a central twist joint realizes the relative rotation between the two segments. We also develop a quasi-static kinematic model relating the segment rolling speeds to the linear and angular velocities of the robot.

Real-robot experiments demonstrate the various motion modes, traversal through a 10 cm clearance test track, and maneuvering tasks beneath a large workpiece and a car chassis.

In these low-clearance scenarios, S-rolling successfully performs approximately 90$^\circ$ and 180$^\circ$ heading changes, whereas the baseline rolling arc gait cannot change the robot heading.

summary.en: The paper presents S-rolling, a steerable rolling gait for twistable snake robots designed to combine low swept height with planar maneuverability. It uses an S-shaped planar backbone and independently controlled rolling speeds for the head and tail segments; a central twist joint creates their relative rotation. The authors derive a joint-space gait equation and a quasi-static kinematic model. Real-robot experiments demonstrate several motion modes, traversal through a 10 cm clearance track, and turning beneath a workpiece and car chassis. In these settings, the robot makes approximately 90- and 180-degree heading changes, unlike the baseline rolling arc gait.
summary.zh: 论文提出 S-rolling，一种面向可扭转蛇形机器人的可转向滚动步态，旨在兼顾低扫掠高度与平面机动性。该方法采用 S 形平面骨干曲线，并独立控制头尾段的滚动角速度；中央扭转关节实现两段相对旋转。作者推导了关节空间步态方程和准静态运动学模型。真实机器人实验展示了多种运动模式、通过 10 厘米净空测试轨道，以及在大型工件和汽车底盘下方转向；在这些场景中可实现约 90 度和 180 度转向，而基线滚动弧步态无法改变朝向。

sections.text:
Multimodal reasoning provides robotic foundation models with predictive context needed for reliable action generation.

However, language-based reasoning captures task semantics but struggles to express fine-grained physical dynamics, while latent reasoning models future state evolution but offers limited structure for organizing these dynamics into reusable reasoning primitives.

To bridge this gap, we introduce PhysWord, a reasoning-before-acting foundation model built on Physical Words, which use atomic action verbs as shared semantic anchors for continuous representations of physical dynamics.

Specifically, PhysWord predicts upcoming atomic action words and directly aligns their contextual hidden states with latent targets derived from the corresponding future observations. Building on these primitives, we construct a temporally structured PhysWord space with visual and optional tactile variants of each action word.

Autoregressively predicting Physical Words across future timesteps captures transitions between execution stages, providing structured multimodal context for action generation.

PhysWord achieves state-of-the-art success rates of 90.3\% on visuotactile UniVTAC and 99.6\% on vision-based LIBERO-Long, and outperforms competing methods on real-world tasks using bimanual grippers and dexterous hands.

Further evaluations demonstrate that our structured latent reasoning framework generalizes to unseen scenarios and enables long-horizon manipulation. Project page: https://nvidia-isaac.github.io/video_to_data/physicalword/

summary.en: The paper introduces PhysWord, a reasoning-before-acting foundation model for robot manipulation. Its Physical Words use atomic action verbs as semantic anchors for continuous representations of physical dynamics. The model predicts upcoming action words and aligns their contextual hidden states with latent targets derived from future observations. Autoregressive prediction across future timesteps represents transitions between execution stages and provides structured multimodal context for action generation; words have visual and optional tactile variants. The authors report benchmark success rates, stronger performance than competing methods on real-world tasks with bimanual grippers and dexterous hands, and evaluations indicating generalization to unseen scenarios and long-horizon manipulation.

sections.text:
Blind and visually impaired individuals face uncertainty when navigating unfamiliar areas. Whether a cane or a guide dog is used for navigation, this may prove to be challenging.

To mitigate this challenge, we present the Context-Aware Navigation Explanation framework that explains guide dog movements for obstacle avoidance and navigation using a large language model. This system integrates perceptual context with planned future trajectories to generate natural-language explanations of robot movement.

We deploy the system on a Unitree Go2 platform in indoor navigation scenarios and evaluate how different explanation context configurations affect user trust and explanation satisfaction.

Results show a strong positive relationship between explanation satisfaction and trust, and suggest that combining obstacle information with future trajectory leads to the most effective explanations. These findings highlight the potential of context-aware language explanations to improve transparency and trust in assistive robot navigation.

summary.en: The paper presents a context-aware framework that uses a large language model to explain assistive robot movements for obstacle avoidance and navigation. It combines perceptual context with planned future trajectories and is deployed on a Unitree Go2 in indoor navigation scenarios. The evaluation examines how explanation context affects user trust and satisfaction. The reported results show a strong positive relationship between satisfaction and trust, and suggest that explanations combining obstacle information with future trajectories are most effective.

sections.text:
Force-aware manipulation typically relies on specialized force or tactile sensors. We show that force-aware manipulation can instead be achieved through visual force prediction from the deformation of a compliant Fin Ray gripper. Our approach trains two models.

First, we train a visual force estimator on calibration data and use it to annotate task demonstrations with force estimates. Second, we train an action--force proposal policy on these force-augmented demonstrations to jointly generate candidate robot actions and their associated forces.

At test time, we sample candidate actions and the forces they are expected to produce, then execute the action whose predicted force is closest to a target from the demonstrations. We evaluate our approach on berry picking, empty-can grasping, in-hand reorientation, and plug insertion.

Our results show that visual force prediction can guide inference-time action selection for contact-rich manipulation without requiring force or tactile sensors at deployment.

summary.en: The paper proposes predicting force visually from deformation of a compliant Fin Ray gripper to support contact-rich manipulation without force or tactile sensors at deployment. A visual force estimator annotates task demonstrations, which then train an action-force proposal policy. At test time, the system selects the candidate action whose predicted force is closest to a target from the demonstrations. The approach is evaluated on berry picking, empty-can grasping, in-hand reorientation, and plug insertion; the authors report that visual force prediction can guide inference-time action selection.

sections.text:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models achieve strong performance across embodied manipulation tasks by unifying visual understanding, language conditioning, and action generation.

However, long-horizon tasks can involve non-Markovian dependencies: successful decisions may require retaining task progress and past interaction outcomes, while partial observability and execution errors compound over time.

Existing work has begun to address these challenges by augmenting foundation-model policies with memory and by introducing hierarchical architectures that separate high-level planning from low-level execution.

We organize the high-level VLM as a robotic agent through an editable harness to maintain task context and improve planning through execution experience. We instantiate this approach as SERA (Self-Evolving Robotic Agent), with a fixed VLA executor providing low-level control.

The harness maintains and updates task context using observations and execution feedback to guide subsequent planning. Self-evolution uses environment rollouts to propose and evaluate harness revisions, with the selected configuration fixed before held-out testing.

On RoboMME, SERA achieves 51.38% overall success with autonomous selection, compared with 44.38% without self-evolution. Our exploration suggests that agentic planning is a promising direction for history-dependent robotic manipulation.

summary.en: The paper addresses history-dependent manipulation, where task progress, partial observability, and execution errors affect long-horizon decisions. SERA organizes a high-level vision-language model as a robotic agent through an editable harness, while a fixed VLA executor handles low-level control. The harness updates task context from observations and execution feedback. Environment rollouts propose and evaluate revisions, with the selected configuration fixed before held-out testing. On RoboMME, SERA reports 51.38% overall success with autonomous selection, compared with 44.38% without self-evolution.

sections.text:
Recent advances in frontier AI models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in visual understanding, reasoning, planning, and tool use, raising the possibility of using general-purpose AI models for robot manipulation without task-specific training.

However, their manipulation capabilities have not been systematically evaluated on standardized robotics benchmarks. In this report, we present a unified closed-loop manipulation framework for evaluating frontier AI models on the LIBERO-10 benchmark.

Our framework enables models to control a robot directly through visual observations, robot proprioception, and structured tool calls, primarily by specifying target end-effector poses and gripper commands, without task-specific fine-tuning or pretrained manipulation skills.

We evaluate six frontier AI models, including GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Luna, Claude Opus 5, Claude Opus 5.5, and Gemini-4 Argon, across three reasoning effort levels, resulting in 18 configurations and 1,800 evaluation episodes. Our results show that GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest success rate of 44%, followed by Gemini-4 Argon at 43%.

Increasing reasoning effort generally improves manipulation performance, but the benefits vary across models and come at additional inference cost. We also observe substantial differences across tasks, with models performing relatively well on object placement tasks but struggling with precise spatial arrangements and complex multi-step interactions.

These findings demonstrate both the potential and limitations of frontier AI models for robot manipulation, highlighting the challenges of translating reasoning capabilities into reliable physical actions.

We release our evaluation framework and experimental results to support reproducible benchmarking and future research on reasoning-based robot manipulation.

summary.en: The report introduces a unified closed-loop framework for evaluating general-purpose AI models on LIBERO-10. Models control a robot using visual observations, proprioception, and structured tool calls, without task-specific fine-tuning or pretrained manipulation skills. Six models are assessed at three reasoning effort levels, covering 18 configurations and 1,800 episodes. GPT-6 Astra reports the highest success rate at 44%, followed by Gemini-4 Argon at 43%. Greater reasoning effort generally helps, with model-dependent benefits and added inference cost; performance varies by task.
summary.zh: 报告提出一个用于 LIBERO-10 的闭环操作评估框架，让通用 AI 模型依据视觉观察、机器人本体感知和结构化工具调用控制机器人，主要指定末端执行器目标位姿与夹爪指令，无需任务专用微调或预训练操作技能。研究评估六种前沿模型的三档推理强度，共 18 种配置和 1,800 个评估回合。GPT-6 Astra 成功率最高，为 44%，其次为 Gemini-4 Argon 的 43%。报告称增加推理强度通常有帮助，但收益因模型而异且增加推理成本；模型在物体放置上相对较好，在精确空间排列及复杂多步交互上较弱。

sections.text:
Long-horizon robotic operation requires memory that scales with essential information rather than execution time. We present a parameter-space memory framework where each episode is stored as a separable object.

A neural implicit representation is fitted to episode video from a shared, meta-learned initialization; the resulting weight delta constitutes the memory. Crucially, this delta remains a fixed size regardless of whether the episode spans a hundred or a hundred thousand frames.

A learned projector maps the weight delta into token embeddings, conditioning a language model for question answering and a decoder for joint command regression, without frame retrieval at query time. On RoboMME, the language model exceeds chance across all question types, and the decoder achieves a mean $R^2$ of 0.51.

Replacing the delta with matched noise drops performance by 11.4 points, while random-origin weights are non-decodable, proving the meta-learned initialization is essential for embedding episode content.

By representing individual experiences as fixed-size weight deltas in a common parameter space, this approach decouples memory cost from time horizon and provides a basis for scalable streaming memory.

sections.text:
General-purpose robots must handle tasks, objects and environments they were never trained on, yet zero-shot generalization remains one of the least solved problems in physical AI. In digital AI, zero-shot capability grew with the volume and, above all, the diversity of training data, much of it sourced from the crowd.

Robotics instead relies on paid collection by a few well-funded teams, which yields volume without diversity. We formulate zero-shot generalization in physical AI as coverage of the deployment distribution, and show that more samples from the same collectors shrink the unseen region only slowly, while each new contributor can extend it.

Building on this and on zero-shot learning, we propose a shared latent space for robot actions that combines multi-modal alignment, generative augmentation, and noisy-label learning. As a scalable source of diverse data, we propose a community of developers building applications on one standard, approachable robot, Origami.

We close with a testable hypothesis and an evaluation protocol relating real-robot zero-shot success to the diversity of contributed data.

sections.text:
Safe robotic task planning requires planners that can reliably achieve task goals while satisfying safety constraints. Classical planners search over explicit symbolic task representations and can provide formal guarantees with respect to encoded safety constraints, but require rigid input formats.

Their computational cost also increases rapidly with the search space. In contrast, large language models (LLMs) offer flexible task interfaces and strong generalization capabilities, but they are large, power-hungry, and pre-trained with little robot-specific safety data and knowledge.

Thus, they can be difficult to deploy locally on robotic systems with limited resources. To address these limitations, we present SLoSa, a neuro-symbolic compression and fine-tuning framework for training foundation-model-based robotic task planners with Small size, Low power demand, and Safety awareness.

The framework first constructs a safety-aware dataset using classical planners, an advanced teacher LLM, and formal verifiers, followed by two training stages: supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tuning guided by a verification-based reward machine to enforce safety alignment.

We evaluate SLoSa across four Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL) domains, two household simulation environments, local edge platforms, and a desktop robotic arm.

Across the PDDL tasks, verifier-guided post-training raises the success rate of compact 4B-14B planners to 70.5-76.0%, while INT4 deployment on a Jetson Orin requires 17.85-26.41 W of average power. Results in household simulators and on the physical robot further demonstrate the applicability of SLoSa across diverse robotic task settings.

sections.text:
Traditional robotic navigation systems separate mapping, planning, and low-level control through cascaded modules, introducing computational overhead and accumulated latency. End-to-end reinforcement learning offers a compact unified policy that maps onboard observations directly to control actions.

However, on inherently unstable platforms such as two-wheeled inverted-pendulum robots, navigation progress and obstacle avoidance can conflict with attitude stabilization in a strongly state-dependent manner. We propose a lightweight state-dependent objective coordination method for integrated navigation and control.

A pitch-conditioned scalarization coefficient $\beta(s)\in[0,1]$ adjusts the relative contributions of balance stabilization and navigation objectives during training, without extra control hierarchies or auxiliary attitude-stabilization controllers, such as proportional-integral-derivative (PID) or linear-quadratic regulator (LQR) controllers.

To support zero-shot deployment, simulation training models execution delay, action hold, asynchronous and noisy observations, and dynamics uncertainty. Gradient analysis reveals persistent directional interference and state-dependent variation in the objectives' relative scales.

Comparisons with alternative reward-weighting, constraint, training, and control-structure strategies show that PPO+$\beta(s)$, where PPO denotes proximal policy optimization, achieves 98% and 95% success rates with small attitude excursions on the fixed obstacle map and the randomly generated high-obstacle-density map, respectively.

Zero-shot hardware experiments further demonstrate bounded attitude behavior and consistent obstacle avoidance using only onboard observations. Training and evaluation code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.

summary.en: The paper proposes a lightweight state-dependent objective coordination method for two-wheeled inverted-pendulum robots. A pitch-conditioned coefficient adjusts the balance and navigation objectives in an end-to-end reinforcement-learning policy. Simulation models execution delay, action hold, asynchronous and noisy observations, and dynamics uncertainty. The authors report success rates of 98% on a fixed obstacle map and 95% on a randomly generated high-density map for PPO with the proposed coefficient. Zero-shot hardware experiments show bounded attitude behavior and consistent obstacle avoidance using onboard observations.

sections.text:
Vision-language-action (VLA) policies need to recognize gaps in their training knowledge to request useful demonstrations or assistance in new situations, especially when failures are costly. Disagreement within an ensemble of independently trained policies can guide these decisions, but requires training and running multiple policies.

We propose post-hoc kernel-variance heads that estimate epistemic uncertainty from the embeddings of a single policy. Each head computes the conditional variance of a Gaussian process conditioned on embeddings from the training demonstrations. Fitting requires no regression targets or gradient updates and leaves the policy unchanged.

In experiments with SmolVLA on LIBERO-10, the kernel variance heads perform competitively with two-policy ensemble scores in task-level correlation with task success, in demonstration acquisition during active learning, and in referral to a stronger supervisor policy as a proxy for human assistance.

For SmolVLA, the head on the vision-language backbone reduces uncertainty-scoring time by up to approximately a factor of 50 compared with ensemble scores, while also substantially reducing setup costs.

We also show that the established evaluation protocol on LIBERO-10 primarily rewards recognition of coverage differences between tasks, while execution variability weakens assessment of within-task rankings.

Thus, controlled perturbations provide a complementary evaluation: modality-specific heads identify unfamiliar camera, instruction, or state inputs, while fused heads can detect unfamiliar combinations of individually familiar inputs.

With a supervisor proxy trained on the evaluated perturbation families, the decoder head improves within-task referral over ensemble disagreement. These findings show that useful uncertainty estimates for adaptive robot learning can be obtained from a single policy.

summary.en: The paper proposes post-hoc kernel-variance heads that estimate epistemic uncertainty from embeddings of a single vision-language-action policy. Fitting uses no regression targets or gradient updates and leaves the policy unchanged. In SmolVLA experiments on LIBERO-10, the heads perform competitively with two-policy ensemble scores for task-success correlation, active-learning demonstration acquisition, and referral to a stronger supervisor. The authors report that a head on the vision-language backbone cuts uncertainty-scoring time by up to about 50 times. They also use controlled perturbations to complement the established evaluation protocol.

sections.text:
Agricultural robots are serving as powerful members across a wide range of tasks, nevertheless, they are still heavily relying on manual operations or railway systems for movement.

In contrast, Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) enables navigating robots from starting points to target positions following natural language instructions, having shown strong performances across various domains. However, none of the existing benchmarks or methods are specifically designed for agricultural robots.

To bridge this gap, we build our A2A benchmark, which consists of 1,560 episodes across 6 classes of agricultural scenes using the step-by-step format for instructions and the continuous environment for actions.

We evaluate several existing state-of-the-art VLN methods on A2A, then we observe that they perform well on short instructions while perform poorly on long instructions.

To alleviate this phenomenon, we design our STL module, which decomposes a complex instruction into a list of simple subtasks, thereby assisting the decision-maker to focus on the current short subtask rather than the entire long instruction at any time.

We integrate STL into the NavGPT backbone to propose our AgriVLN method, achieving a sufficient improvement on SR from 0.33 to 0.47 with a slight sacrifice on NE from 2.76 m to 2.91 m. We further implement the ablation studies and the case study, discussing the effectiveness and limitations of AgriVLN on different subtask quantities and scene classes.

Repository: https://github.com/AlexTraveling/AgriVLN.

summary.en: The paper introduces A2A, a vision-and-language navigation benchmark for agricultural robots with 1,560 episodes across six agricultural scene classes, step-by-step instructions, and continuous actions. Evaluations find that existing methods handle short instructions well but perform poorly on long ones. The authors propose STL, which decomposes complex instructions into simple subtasks, and integrate it with the NavGPT backbone as AgriVLN. They report that success rate rises from 0.33 to 0.47, while navigation error changes from 2.76 m to 2.91 m. Ablations and case studies examine effects and limitations across subtask counts and scene classes.

sections.text:
This paper presents a novel framework integrating a robust wrench observer with a hybrid pose and force controller for physical Human-Robot Interaction (pHRI).In pHRI tasks, robots are expected to perform task-space motions robustly while remaining compliance with human disturbance, which proposes distinct control objectives.

Most existing approaches focus mainly on either robustness or compliance and rely on force sensors for real-time tracking. To address these limitations, we propose a novel framework with the following key contributions. Firstly, a neural network (NN) is trained to improve the observer performance by compensating for system friction and unmodeled dynamics.

Secondly, a task-null-space decomposition is applied to separate the joint velocity and reduce the effect of the human disturbance on the observer. Finally, a hybrid pose and force controller is introduced to achieve the end-effector pose and force tracking.

Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework provides robust and accurate wrench estimation while maintaining reliable pose and force tracking performance.

The proposed approach offers an effective solution and framework for pHRI without the need of force/torque sensor measurements which can be applied to many robotic manipulator platforms which do not have force/torque sensors.

summary.en: The paper presents a framework for physical human-robot interaction that combines a robust wrench observer with a hybrid pose-and-force controller, without force/torque sensor measurements. A neural network compensates for friction and unmodeled dynamics, while task-null-space decomposition is used to reduce the effect of human disturbance on the observer. The authors report experimental results showing robust wrench estimation and reliable pose and force tracking. These claims are based on the reported experiments.

sections.text:
Industries employ robots for repetitive tasks due to their high precision and performance, typically achieved through feedforward control actions based on an accurate robot description. However, an exact dynamic model can be difficult to obtain, especially for robots with elastic elements or when the payload changes.

Learning-based feedforward approaches are promising for trajectory tracking under model uncertainties, but typically face generalization issues when task parameters vary. This paper proposes a novel method to generalize the feedforward control action with respect to payload parameters, independently of the underlying controller.

Firstly, the minimal number of example objects needed for payload generalization is derived. Then, an algorithm is proposed to execute the same trajectory with a new payload, given only its parameters, without knowledge of the robot's dynamic model and even in the presence of elastic joints.

The effectiveness of the proposed algorithm is validated in simulations and experiments on tracking tasks with different robots and controllers. Two sets of experiments are performed: on a standard Franka Emika Panda robot, and on a Franka Emika Panda robot equipped with an elastic wrist.

summary.en: This paper proposes a learning-based method for generalizing feedforward control actions across payload parameters, independently of the underlying controller. The authors derive the minimum number of example objects needed for payload generalization and present an algorithm for executing the same trajectory with a new payload using only its parameters. The method does not require knowledge of the robot’s dynamic model and is intended to cover robots with elastic joints. Its effectiveness is evaluated in simulations and tracking experiments with different robots and controllers, including two Panda configurations.

sections.text:
Automated progress monitoring on construction sites is an active area of research and development. Robot and human-carried mapping systems have been developed to build 3D maps of building and infrastructure projects. While LiDAR-based mapping systems achieve high accuracy, the cost of LiDAR can be prohibitive.

Consumer-grade cameras with wide field of view ("360 cameras") combined with embedded inertial measurement units (IMUs) provide a cost-effective alternative. To support change detection and progress monitoring, highly accurate visual simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) and floor plan localization systems are required.

In this paper, we present a high-quality dataset collected at an active construction site, which captures realistic challenges such as variable lighting conditions, moving workers, fast motions, and repetitive structures. The dataset offers thirty visual-inertial sequences recorded across ten floors over an eight-month period of the construction project.

Ground truth trajectories are collected using a high quality LiDAR-inertial SLAM system rigidly attached to the 360 camera. Additionally, we report the results of an open research challenge evaluating the best visual SLAM and localization systems from around the world.

The Challenge attracted substantially higher participation in SLAM, with 62 teams compared to 22 in floor plan localization, which suggests that this task receives less attention from researchers and motivates further exploration through proposed dataset and challenge, available at: https://hilti-trimble-challenge.com/dataset-2026.

summary.en: The paper introduces a visual-inertial dataset collected at an active construction site to support research on SLAM and floor plan localization using 360-degree cameras and IMUs. It includes thirty sequences across ten floors, recorded over an eight-month project period, with conditions such as variable lighting, moving workers, fast motion, and repetitive structures. Ground-truth trajectories were collected using a LiDAR-inertial SLAM system attached to the camera. The authors also report challenge participation, noting more teams for SLAM than for floor plan localization.

sections.text:
Human video scales easily and does not need robot hardware, but existing methods require depth sensing, overlay the robot onto 2D video, or generate data only for the demonstrated objects.

We present Real2Sem2Real (R2Sem2R), a real-to-semantic-to-real pipeline that turns one monocular RGB video of a human demonstration into thousands of robot demonstrations across the semantic object instances of a category.

R2Sem2R tracks the SE（3） pose of each object with DINOv3-distilled Gaussian splats, outperforming existing methods and FoundationPose with estimated metric depth. R2Sem2R then aligns digital cousins, each generated from one or a few photographs, to the demonstrated objects with a semantic alignment.

This alignment matches whole objects and the functional regions of target objects, such as a coffee machine's tray. R2Sem2R maps the human hand to a feasible robot grasp that extends to the cousins.

Robot demonstrations are generated either in IsaacSim, for photorealistic rendering, or MuJoCo, for contact physics, and R2Sem2R can generate over 2,000 episodes in about two hours.

On two real robots and four tasks, we train a vision-language-action policy on data from one human video per task, and policies trained on our data match or exceed policies trained on teleoperation across diverse object instances. The project page is available at https://real2sem2real.github.io/.

sections.text:
Humanoid fall recovery requires selecting a motion that suits both the surrounding scene and the task. The same fallen pose can admit several ways to stand, with different routes, support transitions, and final headings. Yet reliable recovery alone does not provide control over which of these alternatives the robot executes.

Steering this choice requires anticipating the physical consequences of a requested movement. We present RISE, an approach to perceptive humanoid recovery that lets task objectives steer how the robot returns to standing at inference time.

It builds on two insights: diverse recoveries can be composed from shared movements, and anticipating how these movements unfold allows recovery to be steered toward a task objective. We learn a recovery vocabulary that connects intended movements to motor actions through sensory feedback.

A visual diffusion planner learns from executions of this vocabulary to predict motion intent as future body states. Task costs guide this prediction toward a desired heading, rise speed, or path. The planner then generates motion latents conditioned on the steered intent, allowing the requested movement to shape its execution.

Simulation experiments demonstrate diverse recoveries, terrain adaptation, and test-time steering without retraining, complemented by real-world demonstrations on a Unitree G1.Project page: https://osheraz.github.io/RISE/

items.title: Test-Time Motion Steering for Perceptive Humanoid Fall Recovery

sections.text:
Sequential decision-making under partial observability is difficult because agents must explore to infer hidden, task-relevant information before acting effectively.

Learning such information-gathering behaviors tabula rasa via online reinforcement learning is sample-inefficient, whereas offline imitation averages expert actions across hidden states and fails to learn exploration. In this work, we propose ASTEROID, a simple and effective student--teacher supervised learning framework that can learn test-time exploration.

Although a privileged expert never needs to explore, we demonstrate that a history-conditioned student can learn to do so when trained with on-policy contexts: the student first collects on-policy context under partial observability, and the privileged expert provides action labels conditioned on that context.

By distilling expert actions directly conditioned on the student's on-policy history, the student learns to systematically resolve partial observability, i.e., search while uncertain and exploit once the hidden state is revealed.

This enables efficient test-time exploration (similar to Bayesian posterior sampling) without incurring the impractical training-data costs of reinforcement learning.

Across a diverse range of eleven different environments, including discrete exploration benchmarks, robotic manipulation, navigation, and Procgen environments, ASTEROID achieves ~2x higher returns under fixed exploration budgets, uses ~100x fewer interactions than RL baselines, and outperforms frontier models at exploration.

Finally, our method transfers policies trained in simulation to vision-denied real-world robot manipulation, exhibiting efficient exploration and increasing success by +40% over standard distillation. Overall, it provides a simple yet surprisingly effective framework to learn efficient test-time exploration.

items.title: Asymmetric On-Policy Distillation Learns In-Context Exploration

This report describes a laboratory instantiation of a dynamic microsegmentation function for an Internet-of-Things network, specifically a multi-robot network, using a commercial software-defined microsegmentation tool. Fine-grained dynamic segmentation policies are defined, where segments are adapted based on asset functional and health tags.

Automated implementation of the dynamic policies in software is also undertaken. The microsegmentation solution is shown to automatically isolate an indicated threat in real time, while maintaining unaffected operations.

The demonstration indicates that microsegmentation can be implemented in IoT networks, in a way that allows for robust operation in the face of threats and disruptions.
