sections.text:
This paper considers the path planning problem for autonomous exploration of an unknown environment using multiple heterogeneous robots such as drones, wheeled, and legged robots, with different capabilities to traverse complex terrains.

A key challenge there is to intelligently allocate the robots to the unknown areas to be explored and determine the visiting order of those areas subject to traversability constraints, which leads to a large-scale constrained multiple hamiltonian path problem (mHPP) that needs to be quickly and iteratively solved every time when new space is explored.

To address the hallenge, we propose HEHA (Hierarchical Exploration with Heterogeneous Agents) using a recent hierarchical method that decomposes the exploration into global planning and local planning.

The major contribution in HEHA is its global planning, where we propose a new routing algorithm RCH (Routing with Constraints and Heterogeneity) that can quickly find bounded sub-optimal solutions for mHPP to minimize the maximum path length (i.e., makespan) among the agents subject to traversability constraints.

Additionally, the local planner in HEHA also considers heterogeneity to avoid repeated and duplicated exploration among the robots.

The experimental results show, in the presence of heterogeneous traversability, our RCH can solve mHPP with up to 47% smaller makespan than several baselines, and HEHA can reduce the exploration time by up to 30% compared with existing approaches.

items.title: HEHA: Bounded Suboptimal Planning for Constrained Routing and Its Use in Heterogeneous Multi-Robot Exploration of Unknown Environments

We explore how scalable robot data can address real-world challenges for generalized robotic manipulation. Introducing AgiBot World, a large-scale platform comprising over 1 million trajectories across 217 tasks in five deployment scenarios, we achieve an order-of-magnitude increase in data scale compared to existing datasets.

Accelerated by a standardized collection pipeline with human-in-the-loop verification, AgiBot World guarantees high-quality and diverse data distribution. It is extensible from grippers to dexterous hands and visuo-tactile sensors for fine-grained skill acquisition.

Building on top of data, we introduce Genie Operator-1 (GO-1), a novel generalist policy that leverages latent action representations to maximize data utilization, demonstrating predictable performance scaling with increased data volume.

Policies pre-trained on our dataset achieve an average performance improvement of 30% over those trained on Open X-Embodiment, both in in-domain and out-of-distribution scenarios. GO-1 exhibits exceptional capability in real-world dexterous and long-horizon tasks, achieving over 60% success rate on complex tasks and outperforming prior RDT approach by 32%.

By open-sourcing the dataset, tools, and models, we aim to democratize access to large-scale, high-quality robot data, advancing the pursuit of scalable and general-purpose intelligence.

items.title: AgiBot World Colosseo: A Large-scale Manipulation Platform for Scalable and Intelligent Embodied Systems

sections.text:
Autonomous mobile robots require spatial representations that capture geometry and semantics while staying sparse enough for planning in large, unknown environments. Graphs provide a natural representation for this purpose and underpin both classical planning methods and a growing class of reinforcement-learning (RL) policies.

However, RL training needs hundreds to thousands of parallel environments, each constructing and updating its own graph. Existing graph libraries are typically designed for either single-robot deployment or fixed graphs, and CPU-based graph construction limits scalable training to only a few dozen environments.

We introduce GGraph, an open-source GPU-accelerated graph library for both robot deployment and large-scale learning. GGraph supports real robots through ROS 2 interfaces and vectorized GPU-based policy training, with built-in support for tasks including 3-D navigation, exploration, and loop-closure integration.

For single-robot operation, GGraph updates graphs in milliseconds. At scale, it enables graph-based exploration policies to train across hundreds of parallel robots, reducing wall-clock training time by one order of magnitude.

Across simulation and real-world experiments, these results establish GGraph as a unified graph infrastructure for both large-scale robot learning and deployment.

items.title: GGraph: A GPU-Accelerated Library for Graph-Based Robot Deployment and Learning

sections.text:
Sidewinding is an efficient gait for snake robots to locomote on various terrains, by undulating the backbone curve and shifting the contact segments along it. However, relying solely on undulatory motion limits the locomotive capability of snake robots, and combining it with twisting motion can improve their speed and robustness.

This hypothesis has recently been verified by the rolling vector approach, which locomotes the robot like a differential-drive car. Yet its twisting is concentrated in a short buffer segment, imposing most of the workload on the two twist joints in the middle, which can often overburden the motors and limit its locomotion.

With that in mind, this paper develops a new family of twisting sidewinding gaits that distribute the workload over the entire body with our proposed linear twisting function. Under matched turning speed and total output power, our gaits reduce the peak output power of a single twist joint by 42%.

Real-robot experiments show that, with the reduced workload, our new gaits can locomote the robot in various terrains that the existing rolling vector approach cannot. Besides, our new gaits can move up to 49% faster than conventional sidewinding without twisting.

items.title: Linear Twisting Sidewinding Gaits for Twistable Snake Robot Motion Planning on Complex Terrains

sections.text:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown promise in robotic manipulation, but imitation learning (IL) alone often struggles to master complex long-horizon skills. Reinforcement learning (RL) offers an effective avenue for further improving VLA policies.

However, existing VLA-RL methods typically suffer from delayed and biased credit assignment due to trajectory-level sparse rewards, while imbalanced subtask mastery creates bottlenecks that limit overall performance.

To address these challenges, we propose AtomicRL, an RL post-training framework that leverages atomic task structures for reliable credit assignment and adaptive exploration.

AtomicRL introduces Semantic-Aware Policy Optimization (SAPO), which uses semantic-aware gating to constrain TD residuals from failed atomic subtasks from propagating across task boundaries, mitigating credit contamination while preserving intra-subtask credit assignment and value bootstrapping.

In addition, Bottleneck-Adaptive Target Exploration (BATE) dynamically coordinates task sampling and local exploration incentives based on the mastery of individual atomic subtasks, directing learning toward the remaining bottlenecks.

Finally, we develop a Real2Sim2Real pipeline that bridges online RL in simulation with real-world deployment, facilitating practical transfer to physical robots. On LIBERO-LONG, AtomicRL achieves absolute performance gains of 3.6% and 4.0% over PPO across two VLA architectures. On CALVIN ABC-D, it improves full-task performance by up to 9.5% over PPO.

Combined with the Real2Sim2Real pipeline, AtomicRL further improves real-world task performance by an average of 21.3%.These results demonstrate that AtomicRL effectively improves the learning efficiency and manipulation performance of VLA policies on long-horizon tasks.

items.title: AtomicRL: Atomic Reinforcement Learning for Long-Horizon Robotic Manipulation

sections.text:
Perceptive locomotion policies typically observe a dense robot-centric elevation map, although only the terrain beneath and around the next footsteps informs the control decision. Learned encoders compress the whole visual input, leaving the policy to work out which inputs matter while learning the baseline locomotion task.

Learning both at once slows training and, without computationally expensive attention mechanisms, makes generalization to new terrain harder. We instead remove redundant inputs from the elevation map before the policy sees it.

A lightweight foothold prediction model (FPM) predicts future footholds from proprioception and the velocity command alone, and we sample the elevation map only in small patches around these predicted footholds. We train the prediction model alongside the locomotion policy, periodically retraining it on new policy rollouts as the robot's gait matures.

This allows the perception to anticipate where the policy will step, while the policy learns to leverage terrain information around those steps. With the proposed lightweight preprocessing, the policy reaches a given terrain difficulty in roughly a third of the training iterations required with the complete map.

It outperforms policies that observe the complete map where footholds are sparse, including in narrow walled corridors, and on unseen terrain, and it matches an attention-based encoder trained at several times the cost.

The policy transfers zero-shot to a Unitree G1 humanoid traversing various obstacles, stairs, gaps, and step-downs beyond the training distribution in both indoor and outdoor environments.

items.title: Watch Your Step: Anticipated Perception for Humanoid Locomotion

Recent world action models provide visual foresight and future prediction for robot manipulation, but lack explicit mechanisms for compositional skill reuse. Agentic robotics combines code-based planning and reasoning with reusable skills, but often lacks predictive grounding in physical dynamics.

We introduce AW-0, an agentic world action model framework that integrates code-based planning with joint video and action prediction. We jointly model code, future video, and robot actions as three coupled generative streams within a unified mixture-of-transformers architecture.

Within this architecture a code expert generates parameterized skill routines and control logic while video and action experts generate future visual states and low-level motor commands.

Code serves two complementary roles: it structures multi-step prediction and control within the world model and represents skills as reusable programs for subsequent agentic execution.

We further introduce an automated curation pipeline that labels robot and human video trajectories with aligned programs and consolidates recurring routines into reusable skill libraries.

Evaluations on RoboTwin 2.0 and physical bimanual manipulation tasks show improved task performance over VLA and WAM baselines, alongside gains in language following, semantic reasoning and robustness, demonstrating that agentic code enables connection between planning, prediction and execution within WAMs.

sections.text:
Current Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models rely primarily on RGB perception, preventing them from capturing modalities such as thermal signals that are imperceptible to conventional visual sensors.

Moreover, end-to-end generative policies lack explicit safety constraints, making them fragile when encountering obstacles and novel scenarios outside the training distribution.

To address these limitations, we propose Safe-Night VLA, a multimodal manipulation framework that enables robots to see the unseen while enforcing rigorous safety constraints for thermal-aware manipulation in unstructured environments.

Specifically, Safe-Night VLA integrates long-wave infrared thermal perception into a pre-trained vision-language backbone, enabling semantic reasoning grounded in thermodynamic properties.

To ensure safe execution under out-of-distribution conditions, we incorporate a safety filter via control barrier functions, which provide deterministic workspace constraint enforcement during policy execution.

We validate our framework through real-world experiments on a Franka manipulator, introducing a novel evaluation paradigm featuring temperature-conditioned manipulation, subsurface target localization, and reflection disambiguation, while maintaining constrained execution at inference time.

Results demonstrate that Safe-Night VLA outperforms RGB-only baselines and provide empirical evidence that foundation models can effectively leverage non-visible physical modalities for robust manipulation.

items.title: Safe-Night VLA: Seeing the Unseen via Thermal-Perceptive Vision-Language-Action Models for Safety-Critical Manipulation

sections.text:
Traditional robot programming is notoriously challenging: it requires orchestrating multimodal perception, managing physical contact dynamics, and handling diverse environment configurations and execution failures.

We introduce ASPIRE (Agentic Skill Programming through Iterative Robot Exploration), a continual learning system that autonomously writes and refines robot control programs in a code-as-policy paradigm while compounding experience into a reusable skill library.

ASPIRE operates in an open-ended learning loop, consisting of three components: （1） a closed-loop robot execution engine that exposes fine-grained multimodal traces, enabling the agent to autonomously diagnose failures, synthesize repairs, and validate outcomes; （2） a continually expanding skill library that distills validated fixes into reusable, transferable robotic knowledge; and （3） an evolutionary search procedure that generates diverse programs, systematically debugging them to explore beyond single-trajectory refinement.

ASPIRE surpasses prior methods by up to 77% on manipulation tasks under perturbation, 72% on Robosuite's bimanual handover task, and up to 32% on long-horizon household tasks.

The accumulated skill library further enables zero-shot generalization: on representative unseen long-horizon tasks, ASPIRE achieves 31% success, outperforming the 4% success rate of prior methods. Performance scales with the capabilities of frontier models.

With Claude Opus 5.5, ASPIRE nearly saturates these benchmarks, achieving 99% average success across all 80 LIBERO-Pro tasks and 100% success on representative Robosuite and BEHAVIOR-1K tasks.

Beyond simulation, skills discovered in simulation reduce real-world robot programming effort across embodiments and robot APIs, while skills acquired through online interaction with physical robots enable ASPIRE to solve a Rubik's Cube with progressively improving efficiency.

items.title: ASPIRE: Agentic /Skills Discovery for Robotics

sections.text:
Humanoid loco-manipulation requires an effective interface between high-level task policies and whole-body control. Existing interfaces typically rely on a single action representation for both task intent and whole-body coordination. This may burden the high-level policy or leave one aspect underspecified.

We present SP-HLM, a framework built on a sparse-pose-driven interface. The interface combines five task-critical body poses with a learned latent motion prior to represent spatial intent and whole-body coordination in complementary forms.

SP-VLA, a vision-language-action model, first predicts task-relevant sparse poses and finger joint positions from multimodal observations and language instructions using asynchronous action-chunk inference.

Given these sparse targets, SP-MGM, a motion generation model trained through two-stage distillation, reconstructs coordinated full-body motion in real time. A pretrained motion encoder maps this motion to a compact latent representation.

SP-GMT, a general motion tracker, then integrates the explicit sparse targets with this implicit motion prior for whole-body control. Experiments in simulation and on a real humanoid robot demonstrate improved motion tracking, whole-body coordination, and loco-manipulation success over existing approaches.

Visual world models have shown strong potential for robot planning, yet long-horizon manipulation remains challenging due to compounding prediction errors, large search complexity, and latent plans that the low-level controller cannot reliably reach.

In this work, we introduce Vector-Quantized World Model (VQ-WM), a latent feedback motion planning framework that integrates discrete long-horizon search with continuous visual feedback control: a discrete latent predictor models transitions between vector-quantized latent states, allowing the planner to look far ahead and find a shortest path to the goal through discrete search and a continuous learned controller sequentially reaches the planned states through visual feedback, correcting deviations to mitigate compounding errors.

Whereas most vector quantization uses Euclidean distance, we use a novel estimator of the first-passage-time as a quasi-metric, which aligns the planning abstraction with the controller's capabilities.

We evaluate on the physical robot manipulation of the Tower of Hanoi puzzle: whereas existing state-of-the-art foundation models (VLAs, WAMs) only succeed when the solution trace in their training dataset, our method achieves 100\% success rate with only short-play data, demonstrate its ability to compose long-horizon solutions beyond the short demonstrated trajectories and execute them reliably.

Our solution also outperforms strongest world-models by 13.3--85.3 percentage points on simulation benchmarks spanning manipulation and locomotion, demonstrating consistent progress and new capabilities.

In human-robot interaction (HRI) tasks, humans may interact with the robot in either an active guiding or passive following state, resulting in distinct control objectives for each interaction mode. Most existing approaches rely on predefined switching thresholds to distinguish interaction modes, but their performance can be sensitive to measurement noise.

To address this limitation, we propose a novel framework with the following key contributions. First, a neural network (NN) trained via meta-learning is developed to recognize human intention without manually defined thresholds.

By successfully incorporating force-dependent parameters from the controller, the recognition rates are improved from 90.1\% to 99.1\% for the passive mode and from 79.8\% to 97.1\% for the active mode. Second, an adaptive meta-learning controller is introduced to compensate for human disturbances and enable online adaptation to varying interaction forces.

Third, a multiple-trajectory meta-learning algorithm is designed to jointly learn an environment-basis representation and force-dependent parameters, allowing the controller to deal with unmodeled dynamics efficiently.

Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves robust and accurate control performance, while providing reliable mode recognition for safe and adaptive physical HRI.

Recent advancements in learning from human demonstration have shown promising results in addressing the scalability and high cost of data collection required to train robust visuomotor policies.

However, existing approaches are often constrained by a reliance on multiview camera setups, depth sensors, or custom hardware, and are typically limited to policy execution from third-person or egocentric cameras.

In this paper, we present WARPED, a framework designed to synthesize realistic wrist-view observations and actions from human demonstration videos to facilitate the training of visuomotor policies using only monocular RGB data. With data collected from an egocentric RGB camera, our system leverages vision foundation models to initialize the interactive scene.

A hand-object interaction pipeline is then employed to track the hand and manipulated object and retarget the trajectories to a robotic end-effector. Lastly, photorealistic wrist-view observations are synthesized via Gaussian Splatting to directly train a robotic policy.

We demonstrate that WARPED achieves success rates comparable to teleoperation on four of five rigid-object tabletop tasks and one articulated-object task, while requiring 4-9x less data collection time.

items.title: WARPED: Wrist-Aligned Rendering for Robot Policy Learning from Egocentric Human Demonstrations

Ultrasound examinations typically follow specific scanning protocols that require navigating through an ordered sequence of anatomical landmarks and target imaging planes. We present a local action-conditioned world model framework for goal plane probe guidance in robotic ultrasound.

Autonomous ultrasound tasks often require large numbers of probe-motion trajectories for training, but collecting high-quality demonstrations is labor-intensive and explicit simulators are difficult to build because ultrasound appearance depends on contact, tissue deformation, and view-dependent acoustic artifacts.

We address this problem with a two-stage model-based learning pipeline. First, a latent conditional diffusion world model predicts future ultrasound observations from recent context frames, probe motions and temporal offset.

Second, a goal-conditioned temporal transformer predicts ordered probe motions and is fine-tuned using rewards from the frozen world model. Experiments on the self-collected dataset show that the world model preserves action-dependent anatomical structure on target-directed scans.

In real-world closed loop experiments, the framework achieves success rates of 70.0\% for carotid guidance and 65.0\% for thyroid guidance. These results demonstrate the potential of learned ultrasound dynamics for training goal-directed robotic probe navigation within protocol-constrained organ specific tasks.

Mobile manipulators must navigate safely in cluttered, partially unknown environments across logistics, manufacturing, and service applications. Semi-static changes between robot visits can lead to outdated scene knowledge and increased collision risk.

We propose an active perception framework that enables a high degree-of-freedom (DoF) mobile manipulator to inspect uncertain or safety-critical regions with its hand camera during navigation.

A probabilistic, object- and task-aware next-best-view (NBV) formulation prioritizes observations near the desired path and around uncertain or potentially changing objects.

The perception objective is integrated into hierarchical-task model predictive control (HTMPC), exploiting kinematic redundancy for viewpoint adjustment while preserving the higher priority of base-trajectory tracking. The system unifies navigation, map maintenance, and active perception in a closed loop.

Real-world tests show improved map consistency, reduced task-dependent map entropy, and lower navigation risk than passive or non-task-aware baselines. Additional simulation and real-world sequences demonstrate responses to controlled semi-static scene changes.

Safe control is a prerequisite for real-world embodied intelligence, for which safe reinforcement learning has emerged as a promising paradigm. However, existing safe reinforcement learning methods either require costly real-world exploration or depend on hand-crafted safety functions.

Neither scales to vision-language-action models deployed in open-world physical environments. We propose SafeDojo, a model-based safe reinforcement learning framework that improves vision-language-action policies through world-model imagination. SafeDojo performs online reinforcement learning on top of an interactive video world model.

A ResNet success classifier scores predicted future frames, while a lightweight safety head predicts per-step contact probabilities from the current latent context and proposed action chunk, jointly assessing task execution and trajectory safety. These decoupled signals are balanced through Lagrangian-constrained GRPO.

On SafeLIBERO Level I, SafeDojo improves average safe-success rate by 8.25 percentage points over the strongest baseline; on the zero-shot Level II setting, it is competitive with the strongest model-free baseline. Real-world Franka deployment further shows the best average task and safe-success rates across five tasks.

These results support world-model-based safe reinforcement learning as a promising path toward safer embodied intelligence.

sections.text:
Motivated by the human ability to integrate experience across language, perception, and action, we introduce UniWALM, a unified world-action-language model that learns video, action, and language in a single shared representation, where each modality is both a conditioning signal and a supervision target.

We ask: can jointly generating language enrich this shared representation, improving manipulation and supporting memory-dependent behavior?

Unlike prior approaches that attach a reasoning or vision-language model to a video-action backbone and run them as distinct stages, UniWALM unifies all three modalities inside a single mixture-of-transformers backbone whose per-modality diffusion heads co-denoise synchronously, decoding subtask and textual memory in the same pass as action with no separate planning stage; the generated language is re-consumed on the next step, closing a language-as-memory loop without an external planner or memory bank.

To keep the action stream reliable under this richer objective, we further introduce Flow Matching with Correction (FMC), a training objective that teaches recovery from perturbed action trajectories at no inference-time cost.

UniWALM consistently improves over same-backbone baselines (e.g., FastWAM) on compositional pick-and-place (MolmoSpaces) and across the memory-dependent subset of RMBench, where it reaches 34.5% without any pretrained language or reasoning model and exceeds Mem-0's keyframe-equipped setup (28.5%) using only a single anchor frame.

On a real-world Find-the-Item task, generating textual memory lifts success from 11.1% to 61.1%, while state-of-the-art VLAs stay at or below chance ( < =33.3%).

summary.en: The paper introduces UniWALM, which represents video, action, and language in a shared model and jointly generates actions, subtasks, and textual memory. The generated language is fed back at the next step. It also proposes Flow Matching with Correction, a training objective for recovering from perturbed action trajectories. The authors report improvements over compared baselines on compositional pick-and-place, the memory-dependent subset of RMBench, and a real-world robot search task; textual memory raised reported success from 11.1% to 61.1%.
summary.zh: 论文提出 UniWALM，将视频、动作和语言纳入同一模型与共享表示，并同步生成动作、子任务和文本记忆；生成的语言会在下一步重新输入。作者还提出 FMC 训练目标，使模型学习从受扰动作轨迹中恢复。论文报告，该方法在组合式抓放、RMBench 的记忆相关子集及真实机器人找物任务上优于所比较的基线，并称文本记忆使找物成功率从 11.1% 提升至 61.1%。

sections.text:
Maximum clique and maximum consensus are widely used formulations for robust point cloud registration in robotics. Maximum consensus seeks one transformation that aligns as many matches as possible, while maximum clique selects matches through pairwise distance tests.

Maximum clique is often used as a substitute for or an approximation to maximum consensus, with empirical evidence suggesting a close relationship. However, how closely the two formulations agree is not fully understood. We study this relationship theoretically.

We show that a maximum clique can have arbitrarily large alignment error and be arbitrarily larger than the maximum consensus set at any fixed positive tolerance, and derive geometric conditions that bound this error. When rotation is fixed, we derive sharp error bounds and tests that exactly characterize maximum consensus for the translation subproblem.

Finally, we study group-$k$ consistency, which tests groups of $k$ matches, and determine the smallest group sizes that guarantee alignment error bounds independent of point cloud scale and geometry. These are $d+1$ for rotations and translations and $d+2$ when reflections are allowed, in dimensions $d\ge 2$.

Interactive examples and proof verification using the Lean theorem prover are available at https://ariarobotics.github.io/mc-vs-mc-registration/.

summary.en: The paper theoretically studies the relationship between maximum clique and maximum consensus in point cloud registration. It shows that a maximum clique may have arbitrarily large alignment error and may be arbitrarily larger than the maximum consensus set at any fixed positive tolerance, while deriving geometric conditions that bound the error. For fixed rotation, it gives sharp error bounds and tests that exactly characterize maximum consensus for translation. It also identifies group sizes that guarantee scale- and geometry-independent alignment error bounds.
summary.zh: 论文从理论上研究点云配准中最大团与最大一致集的关系。作者证明，最大团可能具有任意大的对齐误差，也可能远大于任意固定正容差下的最大一致集，并给出限制误差的几何条件。旋转固定时，论文推导了误差界及精确刻画平移子问题最大一致集的检验方法；还确定了群组一致性保证尺度与几何无关误差界所需的最小匹配组大小。

items.title: On Maximum Clique and Maximum Consensus Formulations in Point Cloud Registration

sections.text:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models are sensitive to visual corruptions, but knowing that a corruption is typically harmful does not establish whether removing it would benefit the current episode.

Furthermore, when several corruptions co-occur, deciding what to correct requires understanding which ones contribute to failure risk and how much their removal would help. We define this problem as failure attribution.

Detecting corruption presence alone cannot answer this question, as corruptions can be present but relatively harmless, while directly measuring removal benefits requires costly paired policy rollouts with and without the corruption present.

To address this, we introduce a factorized risk model that learns separate representations of the scene and corruptions, allowing us to estimate removal benefits through latent intervention from the current image and task instruction, without paired clean images or additional counterfactual rollouts.

We evaluate our approach on OpenVLA and $\pi_{0.5}$ in simulation and $\pi_{0.5}$-DROID on a Franka robot. Our method outperforms monolithic and vision-language-model (VLM) baselines, including achieving approximately 3x lower attribution error than frontier VLMs.

We also demonstrate our method adapts to execution context and corruption intensity, and can be used for online failure monitoring on hardware.

summary.en: The paper defines failure attribution for vision-language-action models as estimating which visual corruptions increase failure risk in the current episode and how much their removal may help. Its factorized risk model represents scenes and corruptions separately and estimates removal benefits through latent intervention, without paired clean images or additional counterfactual rollouts. Evaluations use simulation and a Franka robot. The authors report better performance than monolithic and vision-language-model baselines, with attribution error approximately one-third that of frontier VLMs, and demonstrate adaptation to execution context and corruption intensity, plus online hardware monitoring.
summary.zh: 论文将视觉语言动作模型中的失效归因定义为：判断当前图像中的哪些视觉污染会增加失败风险，以及移除它们可能带来多大收益。作者提出因子化风险模型，分别表示场景与污染，并通过潜在干预估计移除收益，无需配对的干净图像或额外反事实策略运行。论文在仿真和 Franka 机器人上评估方法，报告其优于单体模型及视觉语言模型基线，并称归因误差约为前沿视觉语言模型的三分之一；还展示了对执行情境和污染强度的适应及硬件在线监测用途。

items.title: What Would Removing This Corruption Change? Failure Attribution for Vision-Language-Action Models

sections.text:
We study multi-robot motion planning in a polygonal environment with polygonal robots. The setting of the problem consists of a polygonal domain $\mathcal{W}$ with $n$ vertices and $k$ robots $R_1,\dots,R_k$ translating in $\mathcal{W}$ each of which is represented by a polygon of constant complexity.

Given a source configuration $\mathbf{s}$ and a target configuration $\mathbf{t}$ of the robots in $\mathcal{W}$, the goal of the problem is to find a collision-free motion plan from $\mathbf{s}$ to $\mathbf{t}$ that is shortest with respect to some cost function.

We present the first fully polynomial-time approximation schemes (FPTAS) for motion planning with any fixed number $k$ of robots, under the min-sum objective, the min-max objective, and the min-makespan objective.

Here, the min-sum variant aims to minimize the total traveling distance of all robots, the min-max variant aims to minimize the maximum traveling distance of a single robot, and the min-makespan variant aims to minimize the total time cost under the assumption that all robots move with a maximum speed $1$.

The algorithm directly generalizes to the problem in any fixed dimension $d$, with a polytope environment and polytope robots.

Our result settles an open question of Agarwal, Halperin, Sharir, Steiger [SODA'24] and Agarwal, Holmgren, Steiger [SODA'26], who gave an FPTAS for $k=2$ unit-square robots and a bicriteria-approximation algorithm for a fixed number $k$ of unit-square or unit-disk robots, respectively. Compared to the previous results, our algorithm is substantially simpler.

summary.en: The paper studies collision-free motion planning for a fixed number of polygonal robots in polygonal environments. It presents fully polynomial-time approximation schemes for minimizing total travel distance, the maximum distance traveled by any one robot, and total time assuming a maximum speed of one. The authors state that the algorithm extends to fixed-dimensional settings with polytope environments and robots, settles an open question raised by prior work, and is substantially simpler than previous results.
summary.zh: 论文研究多边形环境中固定数量多边形机器人的无碰撞路径规划，提出适用于任意固定机器人数量的全多项式时间近似方案，分别优化总行驶距离、单个机器人最大行驶距离及最大速度为1时的总时间成本。作者称，算法可推广到固定维度的多面体环境与机器人，并解决了先前工作提出的开放问题；相较既有结果，算法更简单。

sections.text:
Collaborative perception enables agents to retrieve the scene semantics and geometry beyond the field of view of any individual agent. This broader scene understanding enhances transportation safety and improves efficiency in multi-robot systems.

However, existing collaborative semantic occupancy methods rely on dense 3D voxel annotations and are limited to recognizing objects within a predefined set of semantic classes. To overcome these limitations, we present CoGaussian, an open-vocabulary Gaussian-based collaborative semantic occupancy prediction framework.

CoGaussian represents a scene as a set of foundation model-aligned sparse 3D Gaussians, which serve as a compact representation for communicating and fusing geometric and semantic information across multiple agents.

On the Semantic-OPV2V benchmark, our method outperforms existing open-vocabulary single-agent approaches, highlighting the effectiveness of open-vocabulary collaborative scene understanding.

summary.en: The paper introduces CoGaussian, an open-vocabulary Gaussian-based framework for collaborative semantic occupancy prediction. It is intended to address the reliance of existing methods on dense 3D voxel annotations and predefined semantic classes. CoGaussian represents scenes as sparse 3D Gaussians aligned with foundation models, providing a compact representation for communicating and fusing geometry and semantics across agents. On the Semantic-OPV2V benchmark, the authors report that their method outperforms existing open-vocabulary single-agent approaches.

sections.text:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies increasingly rely on asynchronous inference to hide model latency behind ongoing robot motion. During inference, the robot continues executing its current action chunk while the next chunk is generated from the observation available at inference start.

By the time the new chunk is executed, the robot or scene may have changed, so an action that fits the prediction-time state can be misaligned with the execution-time state.

Training-time methods modify the policy input or supervised target based on the expected execution delay, but do not directly supervise how actions should change as the scene evolves between prediction and execution.

Runtime repair methods improve chunk continuity or modify actions during deployment, but can still leave actions aligned with the prediction-time state rather than the execution-time state.

Our key insight is that execution-time observations are unavailable when the online prediction is made but are available in recorded trajectories during offline training, making the prediction-execution mismatch observable during training.

We propose DEFLECT, an offline post-training framework that turns this temporal contrast into preference supervision for a policy acting from stale inputs. Across Kinetix, LIBERO, and three real-robot tasks, DEFLECT improves delay robustness across the evaluated VLA policies and settings.

At the longest supported delay, it improves success by 4.2 percentage points over VLASH on Kinetix and by 22.7 points over naive asynchronous execution with GR00T N1.7 on LIBERO.

summary.en: The paper presents DEFLECT, an offline post-training framework that uses differences between prediction-time and execution-time states in recorded trajectories to provide preference supervision for policies acting on stale inputs. The authors report improved delay robustness across evaluated policies and settings on Kinetix, LIBERO, and three real-robot tasks. At the longest supported delay, they report success improvements over VLASH on Kinetix and over naive asynchronous execution with GR00T N1.7 on LIBERO.
summary.zh: 论文提出 DEFLECT，一种离线后训练框架，利用记录轨迹中预测与执行时状态的差异，为使用过时输入的策略提供偏好监督，以应对异步视觉语言动作策略中的延迟。作者报告，该方法在 Kinetix、LIBERO 和三项真实机器人任务的评估中提升了延迟鲁棒性；在所述最长延迟下，相较 VLASH 和 GR00T N1.7 的朴素异步执行取得了成功率提升。

sections.text:
Action-free videos are an appealing substitute for costly teleoperated data. Latent action models (LAMs) turn videos into a supervision signal by inferring abstract actions between frames. Existing LAMs observe a single camera view, which resolves 6D robot actions only ambiguously missing out-of-plane movements and potential occlusions.

We propose a LAM that ingests synchronized multi-camera views using cross-attention to resolve depth and occlusions before compressing them into latent actions. The latent actions are fed into a policy in which a latent expert and an action expert are coupled by sequential flow matching around a frozen VLM backbone.

We further evaluate in strict cross-embodiment settings where task-specific demonstrations come from other embodiments. We show that dual-view LAM pretraining improves the decodability of ground-truth 6D actions by 17% compared to single-view, while scaling single-view data by two orders of magnitude is not sufficient to fully recover out-of-plane motions.

The downstream policy improves success rate by +13.5% compared to +6.2% for single-view LAM. A single cross-embodiment is sufficient for skill transfer, and adding a second viewpoint outperforms adding up to four further embodiments.

The results transfer to hardware where demonstrations come from a human hand improving success rate by +20% over action-only policies in 850 rollouts. We show that video and robot data are complementary, and that benefits of learning from video are task-dependent. Website: https://learnsyslab.github.io/multiview_latent_action_pretraining/

summary.en: The paper proposes a multi-view latent action model that combines synchronized camera views with cross-attention to address depth and occlusion ambiguities in single-view video. Its latent actions support policy learning with a frozen vision-language backbone. In strict cross-embodiment evaluations, the authors report improved decoding of ground-truth 6D actions and higher downstream success than with single-view pretraining. Hardware results using demonstrations from a human hand are also reported; the authors find video and robot data complementary, with video-learning benefits depending on the task.
summary.zh: 论文提出多视角潜在动作预训练方法，利用交叉注意力融合同步摄像机视图，以缓解单视角视频对深度和遮挡信息表达不足的问题，并将潜在动作用于策略学习。作者在跨具身评估中报告，双视角预训练提高了真实六维动作的可解码性，下游策略成功率也优于单视角方法；结果还包括硬件实验，演示来自人手，并显示视频与机器人数据互补，视频学习收益依任务而异。

sections.text:
In recent years, physical artificial intelligence (physical AI) has experienced rapid development, capturing significant attention in academia and industry. However, the field has yet to reach consensus on its definition, technical landscape, and core challenges.

To address this gap, this monograph seeks to define physical AI, present its technical landscape, and examine each key technical subfield in depth. In doing so, it establishes a unified framework for Physical AI: artificial systems that perceive, model, and act upon the physical world through continuous feedback under real-world constraints.

Further, this monograph distinguishes physical AI from conventional digital AI, embodied AI, cyber-physical systems, and digital twins. It develops the foundations of physical AI across physics, control, cognition, learning, and reasoning.

It reviews key methodologies, including multimodal perception, physical data and simulation, world models, embodied foundation models, motor-control systems, multi-agent coordination, and hardware-software co-design. Furthermore, it examines applications spanning robotics, manufacturing, infrastructure, scientific experimentation, and autonomous services.

Particular attention is given to sim-to-real transfer, reliability, real-time execution, evaluation, safety, governance, and long-term deployment.

By connecting perception, prediction, decision-making, action, and adaptation in a closed loop, this monograph identifies the technical challenges and research directions required to advance from narrow automation toward more generalizable physical AI and, ultimately, physical artificial general intelligence (Physical AGI).

summary.en: This monograph aims to define physical AI, describe its technical landscape, and examine its challenges. It characterizes physical AI as artificial systems that perceive, model, and act on the physical world through continuous feedback under real-world constraints. The work distinguishes it from digital AI, embodied AI, cyber-physical systems, and digital twins; reviews foundations and methods across perception, simulation, world models, control, coordination, and hardware-software co-design; and surveys applications. It highlights sim-to-real transfer, reliability, real-time execution, safety, governance, and deployment as concerns for future research.
summary.zh: 这篇专著旨在界定物理人工智能，梳理其技术版图与核心挑战，并将其描述为在现实约束下通过持续反馈感知、建模和作用于物理世界的人工系统。内容区分物理 AI 与数字 AI、具身 AI、信息物理系统及数字孪生，讨论物理、控制、认知、学习和推理基础，并综述感知、仿真、世界模型、控制、协作及软硬件协同等方法和多类应用。作者特别关注仿真到现实迁移、可靠性、实时性、安全与长期部署，并提出研究方向。

sections.text:
Recent advances in visuospatial understanding and agentic reasoning enable direct robotic manipulation with general-purpose multimodal models, but their embodied capabilities remain poorly understood. This paper systematically evaluate GPT-6 Astra for closed-loop robotic manipulation using a lightweight agent execution framework.

We first probe three fundamental embodied capabilities-depth perception, embodied in-context learning, and tactile understanding-and demonstrate that the model can exploit depth information, acquire simple manipulation strategies from contextual demonstrations, and use tactile feedback to correct its actions.

We then evaluate GPT-6 Astra across five established manipulation benchmarks along six capability dimensions.

Despite competitive performance on several benchmarks-26.92\% success on RoboDojo and 76.0\% on RoboTwin 2.0-our analysis reveals a pronounced gap between semantic reasoning and physical execution, particularly in consequence-aware action planning, precision, and complex motion coordination.

To further examine these limitations, we introduce LIBERO-GeoMotion, a new benchmark of geometry-constrained tasks that require precise pose alignment, coordinated translation and rotation, and anticipation of physical action consequences.

GPT-6 Astra achieves only 11.1\% zero-shot success, exposing the difficulty of translating spatial understanding into physically feasible motion.

Real-world experiments corroborate these findings: zero-shot execution is feasible for simple tasks, yet persistent deficits remain in motion feasibility, precise control, and physical safety, while substantial inference latency further hinders practical deployment.

Overall, our results characterize the emerging embodied capabilities of general-purpose multimodal models and delineate the key challenges toward safe, efficient, and reliable robotic manipulation.

summary.en: The paper evaluates GPT-6 Astra for closed-loop robotic manipulation, probing depth perception, learning from contextual demonstrations, and tactile understanding before assessing six capability dimensions across five benchmarks. The authors report that the model can use depth, learn simple strategies from demonstrations, and correct actions with tactile feedback, while identifying a gap between semantic reasoning and physical execution, especially for consequence-aware planning, precision, and coordinated motion. Results on the introduced LIBERO-GeoMotion benchmark and real-world experiments indicate persistent challenges in feasible, precise, and safe control; inference latency also limits practical deployment.
summary.zh: 论文评估 GPT-6 Astra 在闭环机器人操作中的具身能力，先考察深度感知、情境示范中的学习及触觉理解，再在五个基准上分析六类能力。作者报告模型能利用深度信息、从示范学习简单策略并用触觉反馈修正动作，但语义推理与物理执行之间仍有明显差距，尤其涉及后果意识、精度和复杂运动协调。新提出的 LIBERO-GeoMotion 零样本结果及真实机器人实验显示，精确、可行且安全的动作仍具挑战，推理延迟也妨碍实际部署。

sections.text:
Reasoning-augmented vision-language-action (VLA) driving models can perceive and reason about safety-critical hazards yet fail to translate that evidence into safe actions. We characterize this failure as a perception-action binding gap: hazard information is available inside the model but exerts insufficient control over trajectory generation.

Using matched simulated counterfactuals and logged driving replay, we show that in-path hazards are actually encoded in the visual representation, but longitudinal plans are dominated by ego-speed history and respond only weakly to hazard proximity or the model's own reasoning trace.

Further analysis shows that the trajectory generator is capable of braking but sometimes fails to do so due to the perception-action binding gap. Without retraining or modifying any weights, we inject a hazard-conditioned energy into the frozen flow-matching sampler of Alpamayo-1.5, restoring the missing coupling at generation time.

With exact obstacle geometry, guidance cuts footprint intrusion from 58.1% to 14.5% and recovers safe braking whenever sufficient stopping distance remains, eliminating collisions entirely in our braking-relevant closed-loop battery. It also reverses the diagnosed dependence of the plan, from tracking ego speed to responding to obstacle range.

These results separate hazard perception from hazard control in driving VLAs, show that unsafe behavior can arise even when the model has both the evidence and the ability to act on it, and propose a simple fix for bridging this binding gap.

summary.en: The paper describes a perception-action binding gap in reasoning-augmented vision-language-action driving models: hazards may be represented and reasoned about without sufficiently affecting trajectory generation. In simulated counterfactuals and logged driving replay, the authors report that longitudinal plans respond more to ego-speed history than to hazard proximity or reasoning traces. They inject hazard-conditioned guidance into the frozen Alpamayo-1.5 sampler without changing weights. With exact obstacle geometry, they report reduced footprint intrusion and safe braking when stopping distance permits; collision elimination is limited to their braking-relevant closed-loop battery.
summary.zh: 论文指出，推理增强型视觉语言动作驾驶模型可能识别并推理安全隐患，却未将其充分用于轨迹控制。作者将此称为感知—动作绑定缺口，并报告在仿真反事实和记录驾驶回放中，纵向规划更受自车速度历史影响。作者在冻结的 Alpamayo-1.5 采样器中注入风险条件引导，无需改权重；在精确障碍物几何信息下，报告侵入率下降，并在制动距离充足时恢复安全制动。闭环结果限于文中所述的制动相关测试。

sections.text:
Pluralistic alignment requires AI systems to learn from diverse populations whose preferences may reflect heterogeneous or even conflicting objectives, and to personalize their behavior to individual users.

Existing approaches in pluralistic alignment often assume access to annotator identities and rely on powerful pretrained representations to model individual preference variations.

We propose Preference-PCA Pluralistic Learning (P3L), a novel framework for pluralistic alignment that jointly learns trajectory embeddings and the shared basis of preference directions via PCA decomposition from heterogeneous crowd feedback without requiring annotator identities.

At test time, our approach enables rapid and accurate personalized reward learning and downstream policy optimization.

Experiments across multiple embodied control tasks demonstrate that P3L enables steerable personal alignment that generalizes beyond the offline dataset to out-of-distribution new users and attains competitive RL and test performance, while substantially reducing computational cost and supporting variable adaptation query budgets.

summary.en: The paper proposes P3L, a pluralistic alignment framework that learns trajectory embeddings and a shared basis of preference directions from heterogeneous crowd feedback without annotator identities. The authors say it supports rapid personalized reward learning and downstream policy optimization at test time. Experiments across multiple embodied control tasks reportedly show generalization beyond the offline dataset to out-of-distribution new users, competitive RL and test performance, lower computational cost, and support for variable adaptation query budgets. The abstract gives no specific task results or real-world deployment evidence.
summary.zh: 论文提出 P3L，一种从异质群体反馈中学习偏好方向共享基底与轨迹嵌入的多元对齐框架，不需要标注者身份信息。作者称，该方法可在测试时快速学习个性化奖励并优化下游策略。多个具身控制任务的实验显示，P3L 的个性化对齐可推广至离线数据之外的新用户，并取得有竞争力的强化学习和测试表现，同时降低计算成本，支持不同的适应查询预算。摘要未给出具体任务、数值或真实部署结果。

sections.text:
Generalizing manipulation policies across robot embodiments remains difficult because standard policies tie the interactions needed for a task to the actions of a particular robot.

We study zero-shot cross-embodiment manipulation, where a policy trained on source embodiments must be deployed on a structurally different target embodiment without additional task demonstrations.

We introduce Kinematic Interaction Transfer across Embodiments (KITE), which decouples manipulation into embodiment-agnostic interaction prediction and embodiment-specific kinematic decoding, connected through a learned representation of interaction intent based on contact patterns.

An interaction policy is trained to predict the intent using demonstration data only collected on a source robot, and shared across morphologically different target robots. A kinematic decoder realizes these intents by learning from synthetic data generated from each embodiment's kinematic model.

Through such decoupling, KITE can robustly transfer learned skills to a new embodiment given only its kinematic model, without recollecting any task-specific demonstration data. We evaluate KITE on four manipulation tasks in simulation and the real world spanning transfer between parallel grippers, dexterous hands, and composite embodiments.

KITE successfully achieves zero-shot transfer to structurally different target embodiments, and consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Project website: https://kite-manip.github.io/.

summary.en: The paper introduces KITE for zero-shot transfer of manipulation skills to structurally different robot embodiments. It separates embodiment-agnostic interaction-intent prediction from embodiment-specific kinematic decoding. The interaction policy is trained only on demonstrations from a source robot, while decoders learn from synthetic data generated using each embodiment's kinematic model. The authors report that transfer requires only the target's kinematic model, without task-specific demonstrations. Across four manipulation tasks in simulation and the real world, KITE reportedly transfers among parallel grippers, dexterous hands, and composite embodiments, outperforming evaluated baselines.
summary.zh: 论文提出 KITE，用于将操作技能零样本迁移到结构不同的机器人。方法把与具体形态无关的交互意图预测，与依赖机器人形态的运动学解码分开：交互策略仅用源机器人的示范训练，解码器则用各机器人运动学模型生成的合成数据学习。作者称，目标机器人只需提供运动学模型，无需额外任务示范即可迁移技能。在四项仿真及真实世界操作任务中，KITE 实现了跨夹爪、灵巧手和复合形态迁移，并持续优于所比较的基线。

sections.text:
Loco-manipulation has recently shown promising capabilities; however, achieving high-precision control, managing the high-dimensional action space induced by many degrees of freedom (DoFs), and fully exploiting the inherent redundancy of whole-body systems remain challenging.

In this paper, we propose a novel whole-body control framework that effectively addresses these challenges by decomposing the complex loco-manipulation problem into partial reference motion generation and low-level imitation control.

We introduce a new Kinematic Normalizing Flow (KNF) model, trained on a large-scale kinematic dataset, that generates diverse partial kinematic references. A high-level controller is then trained to navigate the KNF's latent space to exploit redundant solutions, while a low-level controller learns dynamically consistent motion execution.

We validate our approach on the quadrupedal robot equipped with a six-DoF robotic arm. In simulation, PAKE outperforms the evaluated baselines in tracking accuracy and feasible workspace coverage on the 4,000-target benchmark. For hardware deployment, we evaluate the system over 24 episodes across 8 different mobile loco-manipulation tasks.

The system achieves end-effector pose-tracking errors of 4.5 cm and 0.14 rad, while maintaining accurate locomotion tracking with linear and angular velocity errors of 0.1 m/s and 0.01 rad/s, respectively.

Our method represents a practical and powerful solution for accurate and generalized whole-body loco-manipulation in high-DoF robotic systems, with promising potential for diverse downstream robotic tasks.

summary.en: The paper proposes PAKE, a whole-body control framework that divides loco-manipulation into partial reference-motion generation and low-level imitation control. Its Kinematic Normalizing Flow model generates varied partial references from a large kinematic dataset; a high-level controller explores redundant solutions in latent space, while a low-level controller learns dynamically consistent execution. The authors evaluate it on a quadruped with a six-DoF arm. In simulation, PAKE outperforms evaluated baselines on tracking accuracy and feasible workspace coverage for a 4,000-target benchmark. Hardware evaluation covers 24 episodes across eight tasks, with reported end-effector and locomotion tracking errors.
summary.zh: 论文提出 PAKE 全身控制框架，将移动操作分为部分参考动作生成和低层模仿控制。其运动学正规化流模型从大规模运动学数据中生成多样的部分运动学参考，高层控制器在潜在空间中搜索冗余解，低层控制器学习动态一致的动作执行。作者在配备六自由度机械臂的四足机器人上验证方法：仿真中，PAKE 在 4,000 目标基准的跟踪精度和可行工作空间覆盖方面优于所测基线；硬件评估覆盖 8 项任务的 24 个回合，并报告末端位姿及行走跟踪误差。

sections.text:
Vision-language-action (VLA) policies are commonly deployed with asynchronous inference in real-world settings, where the next action chunk is generated while the robot is still executing the previous one.

By the time the new chunk is committed, the robot and scene have changed, so the chunk is conditioned on a stale observation and task success drops sharply as this inference delay grows.

Generating multiple candidate chunks could let newer observations inform the final choice, but existing multi-candidate methods either rank candidates with the stale inference-start observation or repeatedly switch between candidates during execution, which can make the executed action sequence discontinuous.

Our key insight is that inference delay can be used as decision time. While candidate generation is still underway, candidate selection can reuse the VLA itself to choose the complete action chunk that best fits a later observation.

We propose PACT-VLA, a training-free framework that generates candidates from the inference-start observation and selects one using this pre-commit observation.

Its scoring function, FlowRes, measures the residual between each candidate's implied flow direction and the velocity predicted by the frozen policy under the pre-commit observation, requiring no separate verifier.

A pipelined implementation overlaps observation processing with candidate generation and batches scoring, so selection adds no control-step delay on the evaluated hardware.

At a four-step delay, PACT-VLA improves average success by 15.0 percentage points over RTC on Kinetix and by 5.2 points over single-candidate asynchronous execution with GR00T N1.7 on LIBERO, and it further improves existing delay-robust methods.

On three real-robot tasks, it raises average success from 60% to 82% over naive asynchronous execution with the same frozen $\pi_{0.5}$ checkpoint.

summary.en: PACT-VLA is a training-free framework for asynchronous robot policies, where action chunks may be based on stale observations. It generates candidates from the inference-start observation, then uses a later pre-commit observation and the frozen policy to select a complete chunk. The authors report higher success on evaluated benchmarks and three real-robot tasks. On the evaluated hardware, the pipelined selection process adds no control-step delay.
summary.zh: 论文提出无训练框架 PACT-VLA，应对机器人异步推理造成的动作块基于过时观测的问题。它在候选动作生成期间获取较新的提交前观测，并用冻结策略评估候选块，选择更匹配当前状态的一整块动作。作者报告，该方法在所评估的仿真基准和三项真实机器人任务中提高了成功率；选择过程在所测硬件上未增加控制步延迟。

items.title: PACT-VLA: Speculative Action-Chunk Verification with Pre-Commit Observations

sections.text:
Developing coordination policies for complex multi-agent systems relies on either labor-intensive algorithm design or opaque task-specific reinforcement learning.

With recent advances in autonomous coding agents, we show that policy search directly in code space offers a compelling third path that combines automated optimization with explicit interpretability.

We investigate a human-directed workflow in which coding agents iteratively propose, implement, evaluate, diagnose, and eventually refine algorithms guided by simulation feedback and explicit correctness verification. We conducted two case studies and found that this workflow robustly outperformed any manually engineered solutions.

On a challenging map in the 2024 League of Robot Runners competition, a two-day search discovered a policy that exceeds the stronger locally reproduced competition entry by 35.0% on the densest instance and generalizes to unseen map instances.

In simulated real-world warehouses with irregular lanes, continuous robot geometry, and asynchronous motion, a week-long search discovered an entirely new class of multi-agent pathfinding algorithm that outperforms a calibrated proprietary solution in throughput by 58.9%.

Under stated assumptions, we further prove that the new algorithm is collision-free and completes, in finite time, every accepted goal that is not withdrawn or replaced.

Together, the studies show that policy search in code space powered by state-of-the-art coding agents offers a highly competitive path to building real engineering solutions that are both effective and analytically tractable.

summary.en: The paper investigates searching for multi-agent pathfinding policies directly in code space, using coding agents to propose, implement, evaluate, diagnose, and refine algorithms under human direction and explicit correctness checks. In two case studies, the authors report that this workflow outperformed manually engineered solutions, including on a competition map and in simulated warehouses. Under stated assumptions, they prove the warehouse algorithm is collision-free and completes accepted goals that are not withdrawn or replaced in finite time.
summary.zh: 论文考察由编码智能体直接在代码空间搜索多智能体路径规划策略的工作流：智能体提出、实现、评估和改进算法，并由人类指导及明确验证正确性。作者报告，两项案例研究中，该工作流优于人工设计方案；其中包括竞赛地图上的策略搜索和模拟仓库中的新算法。作者还在所述假设下证明，该新算法无碰撞，并能有限时间完成未撤回或替换的已接受目标。

sections.text:
Handheld demonstration devices decouple data collection from the robot, but conventional designs burden the hand with a wrist camera, cables and a pose tracker (SLAM, an IMU, a VR controller, or a fixed external camera that the collector's body occludes), and burden the pipeline with as many data streams to timestamp, synchronise and cross-calibrate.

We show that a single egocentric camera (USD 122) worn on the collector's head replaces the wrist camera, the pose tracker and their separate streams with one.

It reads printed fiducials on an electronics-free glove (USD 22) against paper tiles taped around the workspace, giving the 6-DoF gripper pose and the jaw width from the same frames the policy will see; at deployment the same camera rides a low-cost (USD 120) arm beside the robot that mimics the collector's head from the robot's joint state.

Against the robot's encoders the labels are accurate to 6.5 mm and 1.6 degrees median with 93-100% frame coverage, and a policy trained on them instead of encoders pays 3% in validation loss.

Adding 194 glove demonstrations to 48 teleoperated episodes lifts rollout success from 10/25 to 17/25, level with 172 teleoperated episodes alone (18/25), and the full co-trained head-camera policy succeeds in 20/25 against 15/25 for the wrist-camera recipe, whose policies drop the object when the goal leaves their view, and 12/25 for a fixed camera.

summary.en: The paper presents a demonstration setup in which one head-mounted egocentric camera reads fiducials on an electronics-free glove and paper tiles in the workspace. The same frames provide gripper pose and jaw-width labels, while a camera beside the robot recreates the collector’s viewpoint at deployment. The authors report label accuracy and frame coverage relative to robot encoders, as well as validation loss and task success results for policies trained with glove demonstrations in their experimental setup.
summary.zh: 论文介绍一种由单个头戴式第一人称相机读取无电子元件手套和工作区纸质标记的示范采集方案。相机画面同时用于估计夹爪位姿和开口宽度，并在部署时由机器人旁的相机复现采集者视角。作者报告了相对于机器人编码器的标注误差、帧覆盖率，以及加入手套示范后的验证损失和任务成功率；这些结果来自论文所述的实验设置。

sections.text:
Most minimally invasive surgery is still performed with hand-held laparoscopic instruments, and the surgeon's instrument kinematics are lost when the operation ends; only the endoscope video is kept.

This paper presents an end-to-end pipeline that captures this motion in the operating room and uses it to train a surgical robot policy, validated on live animals.

We introduce a surgical instrument-state logger that mounts on the shaft of a standard laparoscopic instrument and recovers its pose and jaw state from an inertial sensor, a time-of-flight sensor and a Hall sensor, with no external camera or tracker.

A data pipeline measures the latency of every sensor channel against a robot ground truth and aligns the channels before forming observation-action pairs.

On these demonstrations we train a diffusion policy with a fine-tuned DINOv3 backbone, selecting its design by closed-loop rollouts in a physics simulator reconstructed from depth maps of an ex-vivo rabbit appendix.

The policy is then retrained on 849 in-vivo demonstrations from four live rabbits and deployed on four additional live rabbits with electrosurgery armed. With the surgeon selecting the surgical phase, the policy completed the appendectomy in three of the four animals.

The results show that demonstrations recorded from a surgeon's own instruments are sufficient to train, select and deploy a bimanual surgical policy in vivo. The robot serves only as the timing reference for sensor calibration and as the executor, and collects no demonstrations.

Both demonstration corpora are released to support future surgical robot learning research.

summary.en: The paper presents a pipeline for learning a bimanual surgical robot policy from demonstrations recorded with hand-held laparoscopic instruments. A shaft-mounted logger estimates instrument pose and jaw state using inertial, time-of-flight, and Hall sensors; robot ground truth is used to calibrate timing, while the robot collects no demonstrations. The authors select a diffusion policy in a physics simulator reconstructed from ex-vivo rabbit appendix depth maps, then retrain it on 849 demonstrations from four live rabbits. With a surgeon choosing the surgical phase, it completes appendectomy in three of four additional live rabbits.

sections.text:
Simulation is a powerful tool for robotics, but building diverse, simulation-ready scenes at scale remains difficult. Reconstructing scenes from single images is a promising alternative, but visual similarity alone is insufficient: objects must also be recovered, accurately placed, and physically grounded.

Existing methods that rely on post-hoc physics settling often misplace objects, producing scenes that look correct but behave poorly under manipulation. We present SceneRig, an agentic system that turns a single image into an editable, simulation-ready scene. SceneRig combines geometric, visual, and physical tools to reconstruct a faithful 3D scene.

An agent then performs edit-and-validate loops inside a physics simulator to achieve physical stability. Across diverse inputs, SceneRig improves instance segmentation, object-centric appearance, and 3D placement while keeping the reconstructed scenes physically stable.

Furthermore, SceneRig is effective for downstream robotics: its scenes predict real-robot policy outcomes more accurately than the baseline method and more reliably support replay of recorded manipulations without trajectory adaptation.

summary.en: SceneRig is an agentic system that converts a single image into an editable, simulation-ready 3D scene. It combines geometric, visual, and physical tools, then uses edit-and-validate loops in a physics simulator to achieve stability. Across diverse inputs, the authors report improvements in instance segmentation, object-centric appearance, and 3D placement while maintaining physical stability. For downstream robotics, SceneRig scenes predict real-robot policy outcomes more accurately than the baseline and support more reliable replay of recorded manipulations without trajectory adaptation.

sections.text:
The integration of dynamic legged locomotion and aerial mobility offers versatility that is deterred by challenges in payload distribution, actuation, and the contrasting requirements of both domains. In this paper, we present the design and operation of a multimodal quadrupedal aerial-legged robot.

The presence of legged aerial systems also allows for thruster-assisted legged locomotion, which we make possible with a unified control framework using Control Contraction Metrics (CCM).

We search for separate domain-specific contraction metrics for walking and flight independently offline and unify them using an online energy-based Control Lyapunov Function Quadratic Program (CLF QP).This enables optimal, cross-domain control allocation, which we show using simulations.

We also show experimental results that validate the mechanical viability of our hardware and the paradigm of thruster-assisted trotting. The stability of said experiments motivates the deployment of the control framework for multimodal operations.

summary.en: The paper presents the design and operation of a multimodal quadrupedal aerial-legged robot, including thruster-assisted legged locomotion. Its unified control framework searches offline for separate Control Contraction Metrics for walking and flight, then uses an online energy-based Control Lyapunov Function quadratic program to combine them for cross-domain control allocation. Simulations demonstrate the control approach. Experiments validate the hardware’s mechanical viability and the thruster-assisted trotting paradigm; their stability motivates deploying the framework for multimodal operations.

sections.text:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models have achieved strong performance on standard robotic manipulation benchmarks. However, their reliability can degrade substantially when task conditions deviate from the nominal setting. Perturbations in object positions and task instructions may lead to complete task failure.

Existing VLA policies generally lack an explicit runtime mechanism for distinguishing these failure modes and selecting an appropriate recovery strategy. To systematically mitigate this issue, we propose FIT-MAC, a failure-aware, closed-loop multi-agent control framework for improving the robustness of VLA policies at inference time.

FIT-MAC augments a VLA policy with an inference-time control layer. First, the Planner Agent parses the language instruction into a structured task specification that captures the manipulation goal and spatial constraints, and the Grounder Agent resolves each instruction-level reference to a visual target.

Next, the Verifier Agent tracks phase-specific execution progress, distinguishes target-binding errors from local execution failures, and determines whether intervention is warranted. The Correction Agent then routes permitted interventions to target rebinding or bounded grasping or placement recovery, depending on the failure type.

When no intervention is required, the pretrained VLA remains the default action generator. Extensive experiments on LIBERO-PRO demonstrate that FIT-MAC improves robustness across multiple VLA backbones, consistently increasing success rates and achieving state-of-the-art performance under diverse perturbations.

summary.en: The paper proposes FIT-MAC, a closed-loop multi-agent control framework intended to improve vision-language-action policy robustness at inference time. Planner, Grounder, and Verifier agents structure instructions, resolve visual targets, track progress, and distinguish target-binding errors from local execution failures. When needed, a Correction Agent selects target rebinding or bounded grasping or placement recovery; otherwise, the pretrained policy remains the action generator. Experiments on LIBERO-PRO report higher success rates across multiple VLA backbones under diverse perturbations and state-of-the-art performance.

sections.text:
Vision-language-action (VLA) robustness is commonly summarized by aggregate task success, which obscures how individual executions change under distribution shifts and where failures emerge in long-horizon tasks.

We introduce \textbf{RoboCasa-Shift}, a diagnostic robustness benchmark built on RoboCasa365 that combines controlled single-factor shifts, matched clean-perturbed rollouts in which each pair shares the same underlying settings and differs only in the target shift, and simulator-grounded stage-aware diagnostics.

We evaluate GR00T N1.5 on four long-horizon tasks that pass a predefined clean-performance gate under four perturbation factors and three calibrated severity levels, including conditions that drive the evaluated policy to complete task failure, totaling 1,040 formal rollouts.

Robustness responses vary substantially across factors and tasks, and increasing severity does not always produce monotonic degradation. For example, one camera condition yields $\Delta\mathrm{SR}=0$ despite 8 of 80 matched episodes changing outcome.

Stage-aware analysis further shows that the same end-to-end degradation can correspond to different execution-depth profiles. Camera $L_2$ and Gaussian blur $L_1$ both yield $\Delta\mathrm{SR}=0.188$, yet their first-stage failure rates are 19.0\% and 36.4\%, respectively.

Our findings suggest that VLA robustness should be viewed as a multi-dimensional property of execution rather than a single end-to-end performance measure, motivating evaluation protocols that jointly capture outcome degradation, paired outcome sensitivity, and failure progression.

The code is publicly available at https://github.com/HaochengWang23/RoboCasa-Shift.

summary.en: The paper introduces RoboCasa-Shift, a benchmark for diagnosing VLA policy robustness in long-horizon household manipulation under distribution shifts. It combines controlled single-factor perturbations, matched clean and perturbed rollouts, and simulator-grounded stage diagnostics. The authors evaluate GR00T N1.5 on four tasks that pass a clean-performance gate. Responses vary by task and perturbation, and greater severity does not always cause monotonic degradation. Stage analysis shows that equal end-to-end degradation can accompany different failure-depth profiles, motivating evaluation of outcome changes, paired sensitivity, and failure progression.
summary.zh: 论文提出 RoboCasa-Shift，用于诊断长时程家庭操作中视觉语言动作策略在分布变化下的稳健性。基准结合单因素扰动、设置匹配且仅目标变化的成对运行，以及基于模拟器的阶段诊断。作者在四项通过干净条件性能门槛的任务上评估 GR00T N1.5；结果显示，不同扰动和任务的稳健性反应差异明显，严重度增加也不总带来单调退化。阶段分析表明，相同的总体成功率变化可能对应不同失败深度，支持同时考察结果退化、配对结果敏感性和失败进程。

sections.text:
Heterogeneous multi-robot task allocation depends on estimates of how suitable individual robots are for candidate tasks, yet suitability can be defined in substantially different ways. We compare ten deterministic methods and two LLM-based variants spanning rule-based, similarity-based, requirement-oriented, fuzzy, and semantic approaches.

Using common robot and task profiles, we compare how the methods score and rank candidate robots, identify feasibility, and select a top robot, while examining how these outcomes change with team composition, scale, spatial context, capability uncertainty, and task representation. The methods frequently disagree despite operating on identical scenarios.

Generic similarity measures can violate properties expected under a one-sided requirement-satisfaction interpretation of suitability, while LLM-based scoring introduces additional stochastic and linguistic sensitivity.

These results show that robot--task suitability should be treated as an explicit modeling choice whose assumptions, robustness, and decision-level consequences should be considered before allocation.

summary.en: The study compares ten deterministic and two LLM-based methods for assessing robot-task suitability in heterogeneous multi-robot allocation. Using common robot and task profiles, it examines scores, rankings, feasibility judgments, and top-robot selections, as well as changes with team composition, scale, spatial context, capability uncertainty, and task representation. The methods often disagree. The authors report that generic similarity measures can conflict with a one-sided requirement-satisfaction interpretation, while LLM-based scores add stochastic and linguistic sensitivity.

sections.text:
Diffusion policies with linearly composed scores have emerged as a promising approach to multitask robotic learning by combining separate factors to enable modular, task-wise adaptation, compositional generalization, and interpretable functional decomposition.

However, current training objectives do not encourage factor specialization, often resulting in uninterpretable denoisers whose composed prediction is an average over identical copies, undermining their architectural premise. To address this, we propose a drop-in score-decorrelation auxiliary loss, motivated by projective composition theory.

Our approach encourages specialization by penalizing overlap directly between component noise predictions, with little architectural change or computational overhead.

We demonstrate across multiple benchmarks that our decorrelation loss consistently reduces measurable double-counting between components, improves task decomposition, and produces behaviorally meaningful specialization without compromising multitask performance. Website: https://al3cl1.github.io/robotics-score-decorrelation.

summary.en: The paper proposes a drop-in score-decorrelation auxiliary loss for diffusion policies that combine scores linearly. The authors argue that existing objectives do not encourage factor specialization, which can produce hard-to-interpret denoisers whose composed prediction averages identical copies. The proposed loss directly penalizes overlap between component noise predictions, with little architectural change or computational overhead. Across multiple benchmarks, the authors report reduced measurable double-counting between components, improved task decomposition, and behaviorally meaningful specialization without compromising multitask performance.
summary.zh: 研究针对线性组合分数的扩散策略提出一种可直接加入训练的分数去相关辅助损失。作者指出，现有训练目标不鼓励各组成因子专门化，可能使去噪器变得难以解释，并让组合预测成为相同副本的平均。新损失直接惩罚不同组件噪声预测之间的重叠，旨在以较少架构改动和计算开销促进专门化。作者报告，在多个基准上，该方法持续减少组件间可测量的重复计数，改善任务分解并产生具有行为意义的专门化，同时未损害多任务表现。
